#3338. Paris start-up Physicl raises $10M to make training data for physical AI

Inovia Capital led the seed round for the start-up, whose customers include Meta, Nvidia, World Labs and Epic Games.

Physicl, a Paris-based start-up that creates training data for AI systems that work in the physical world, has raised $10M in seed funding. Inovia Capital led the round, announced on Friday, with U.S. Venture Partners also taking part.

The company focuses on what researchers call edge cases. These are the unusual situations, such as odd lighting or an unexpected object in the way, where AI models for robots, self-driving cars, and 3D vision often make mistakes.

Its first product, Studio, lets researchers rebuild those situations in 3D. They pick an environment or describe a scene where their model struggles, then change the lighting, the camera angle, and where objects sit.

Studio then produces accurate training data aimed at that specific weakness. As a result, researchers can recreate a failure, test a fix, and measure whether their model has improved.

The platform includes 10,000 3D environments and more than 100,000 objects, which can be combined into billions of different scenes, according to the company.

“Models fail on edge cases. When researchers find these weaknesses, they need a way to generate data that specifically addresses them,” said Alex de Vigan, Physicl’s founder and chief executive.

De Vigan previously founded Nfinite, a Paris company that makes 3D images of products for online retailers and raised $100m in 2022. He has spent six years working on 3D, simulation, and machine learning.

Physicl already works with AI labs and universities, including Meta, World Labs, Epic Games, Amazon Web Services, Nvidia, and the Technical University of Munich.

One customer is SpAItial, a Munich start-up that builds 3D AI models. After adding Physicl’s data to its training set, SpAItial cut the error rate of its room-building model by more than half, the company said.

Physicl will use the capital to grow its team and develop the platform further. It joins a wave of European start-ups working on physical AI, the technology that lets machines understand and act in the real world.

#3337. Canopy Growth (CGC) Q2 2027 Earnings Call Transcript

Margins slipped as Canadian medical reimbursement fell, even as revenue climbed.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Canopy Growth Corporation (CGC -3.58%) reported significant top-line expansion driven by a triple-digit increase in international medical cannabis revenue and the integration of the MTL Cannabis acquisition. Management stated that the company is moving toward adjusted EBITDA positivity in the second half of fiscal 2027 by focusing on cultivation excellence and cost discipline. The company reported a strengthened European supply chain following new certifications, while also addressing margin headwinds in the Canadian medical market. Management indicated that the focus remains on high-quality flower production to satisfy demand in core markets across Canada, Germany, and Poland.

#3336. Apple confirms $7.5 billion bond sale following strong investor demand

Following yesterday’s report that Apple was preparing to raise approximately $7 billion through a bond offering, the company has now finalized terms with the SEC, confirming a slightly larger amount. Here are the details.

Yesterday morning, Apple filed a preliminary prospectus with the SEC, outlining plans to issue a series of bonds maturing between 2028 and 2036.

Soon after, Bloomberg reported that the bond sale was targeting roughly $7 billion, with investor interest already surpassing $30 billion.

Now, Apple has filed the final pricing term sheet for the bond sale with the SEC, confirming a $7.5 billion offering across the seven previously announced series, with the following breakdown:

Floating-rate bonds, as the name implies, have interest rates that fluctuate over time based on certain market conditions, rather than remaining fixed.

Of that $7.5 billion, Apple expects to receive approximately $7.47 billion after deducting underwriting discounts and other offering expenses.

In essence, Apple will pay investors interest over the life of the bonds, then repay the full amount borrowed when each series reaches maturity. Apple may also choose to repay some or all of its fixed-rate bonds early.

As described in yesterday’s prospectus, the company intends to use the proceeds for “general corporate purposes,” which may include stock buybacks, dividends, acquisitions, and debt repayment.

You can read the full filing with the SEC here.

Here’s what I was hoping for from Google’s latest tracker

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I really wanted to love the Fitbit Edge, especially when I unboxed the cute pink version of Google’s latest tracker. I’m a huge fan of the $99 Fitbit Air, which launched earlier this year and immediately became one of the best screenless trackers on the market. Yet after two weeks of wearing the Fitbit Edge, I’m not convinced — here are three things I wish Google had done differently.

Before we dive in, you can read my colleague Dan’s extensive Fitbit Edge review here, as well as our Fitbit Air review on Tom’s Guide.

Let’s start with what I do like about the $180 Fitbit Edge. Firstly, I’m a fan of the design and fit of the tracker: it’s comfortable and unobtrusive on my wrist, especially compared to the likes of the Apple Watch Ultra 4 or Fenix 9 Pro, which I’ve recently been reviewing.

It’s dainty, and Google has done a fantastic job of releasing a huge range of swappable straps to suit every style. If you want a fitness tracker that’ll disappear, this isn’t quite as tiny as the Fitbit Air, but it still ticks that box.

I also think this device is pretty well priced. It’s $80 more than the Fitbit Air, but you’re getting a screen and built-in GPS. If you’re after a sports watch, I’d still recommend looking at something like the Coros Pace 4, which comes in at a similar price point, but for a fitness tracker, you’re getting a decent amount for your money with the Fitbit Edge.

Sure, it’s great to have a physical button on a fitness tracker, and this one is better than the haptic buttons we saw on the Fitbit Charge 6, but I’m a little frustrated by how little the Fitbit Edge’s button actually does.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

For example, you’d expect the button to start a run, not just stop it; instead, you still need to tap the screen before you start moving. Any runner knows nothing’s more frustrating than trying to swipe a touchscreen with sweaty fingers, especially on the start or finish line of a race.

The same applies to the stopwatch feature — you’d expect pressing the button would allow you to start the stopwatch, but instead it takes you back to the home screen. I’m never one to complain about a button on a wearable; in fact, the more buttons, the better, but I’m confused why the Fitbit Edge’s button doesn’t do an awful lot.

One thing missing from the Fitbit Edge compared to its predecessor, the Fitbit Charge 6, is contactless payments. Google says only 1% of Fitbit Charge 6 users utilized this feature, which is why they decided to remove it from the Fitbit Edge, but it still feels like a slightly odd decision in 2026.

Most people will be buying a fitness tracker to track their workouts, and I found a few things missing during my testing. Firstly, you can’t customize the data fields in workout modes or reorder them to see the ones most important to you. Again, this isn’t a deal breaker, but when the screen is that small, it would be nice to prioritize the data fields you care about most.

Secondly, I really wish you could do more when you’re on a walk or run. For example, you can’t use Google Maps navigation in workout modes, which is something I used pretty frequently when running or hiking around a new neighborhood. You also can’t control your music from the Fitbit Edge once you’re in a workout mode, which again, is something I didn’t realize I relied on until it was gone.

It’s also worth flagging that the GPS on the device is automatically set to dynamic, which means it switches between using your phone’s GPS and the built-in GPS. When you switch the tracker to using the built-in GPS, I found it takes a hit on battery life, using around 11% for an hour-long run.

It’s worth noting here that I’m probably not the target audience for the Fitbit Edge. The majority of people who buy this tracker won’t be using it for everyday runs or super-accurate GPS maps.

It’s designed for the casual fitness enthusiast who wants to keep an eye on their daily health metrics, and for that user, it does a great job. If you’re an endurance athlete or a serious runner, there are better devices on the market for you. Plus, if you’re not, a lot of these problems can be solved with a firmware update, so I wouldn’t let it put you off entirely.

#3334. Systems Thinking Is Vital in the Age of AI

Machines can automate drudgery but engineers make key decisions

Sufian Aldogom is an IEEE member, a research affiliate at MIT, and a senior leader at Google in Sunnyvale, Calif.

Modern engineering projects increasingly combine human judgment with machine capability. An engineer can define a problem, then ask an artificial intelligence tool to search relevant research and technical standards, generate design options, test them in simulation, and compare the results. The engineer can then bring the results to specialists who understand the parts AI cannot judge on its own, such as whether a design can be built safely, whether it makes sense in a particular setting, or how it might affect its users. The final decision about whether and how to move forward remains a human responsibility.

AI can help engineers do early project steps that once required several people with different technical skills. The engineer’s role is therefore expanding from performing each technical step to deciding how people, machines, and specialists’ knowledge should work together on the project.

Engineering has always been divided into disciplines, and for good reasons. Electrical, mechanical, civil, software, and other engineering fields require deep knowledge that takes years to develop. AI does not replace that need. It simply changes how easily engineers can explore the parts of a problem that sit outside their own specialty.

Consider a software engineer working on a medical device. AI can help the engineer review relevant biomedical research, understand unfamiliar terms, analyze data, and build an early model.

That does not make the engineer a physician or biomedical expert. It allows the engineer to ask better questions before working with the experts.

The same is true in energy, transportation, manufacturing, and many other fields. A problem might begin as a software issue and then quickly involve hardware, safety measures, economics, human behavior, and regulations.

Engineers do not need to master every field; they need to recognize which expertise the problem requires and bring the right people and tools together.

Systems thinking thus becomes especially important. It requires looking at the whole problem: understanding how its parts affect one another, identifying constraints and failure points, and making trade-offs.

AI adds a new element to the process. Engineers must decide not only how the technical parts fit together but also what work to give to AI, what a person must check, when a specialist should make a decision, and when the problem needs to be redefined.

An engineer’s value is not in knowing everything. It is in knowing how to frame the problem, how to ask the right questions, how to test the answers, and when another expert must lead the project.

This aspect is crucial because technical challenges in engineering are seldom static. As new insights emerge, objectives might shift, unseen limitations can surface, and the initial premise might prove flawed. Rather than rigidly following the starting specifications, an effective engineer adapts and refines the scope as a deeper understanding of the system develops.

Thus, engineering extends beyond mastering technical concepts; it is an adaptable, structured approach to navigating evolving challenges.

New evidence can change the goal, reveal a hidden constraint, or show that the original hypothesis was wrong. Effective engineers go beyond merely acting on the initial problem statement. They update it as the system becomes better understood.

In that sense, engineering is not only a body of technical knowledge, it is also a disciplined way of thinking about a project.

AI can produce convincing answers even when its assumptions are weak. It can generate code that works in one test but fails in another. It can summarize research without understanding which evidence is strongest, or optimize a design for the wrong goal. Such limits make human expertise more important, not less.

Machines are useful where speed, scale, search, pattern recognition, and data generation matter. People are essential where context, values, responsibility, and judgment matter. The challenge is to decide where each belongs.

An AI system might generate several designs for a medical sensor, for example, and predict how each will perform. An engineer can test the predictions and reject designs that violate technical requirements. A clinician can determine whether the sensor can be realistically used. Patients and practitioners might reveal problems that neither the engineer nor the developer considered. The final solution emerges from combining the perspectives.

The engineer is still a builder and specialist but increasingly also a coordinator of knowledge.

An engineer’s value is not in knowing everything. It is in knowing how to frame the problem, how to ask the right questions, how to test the answers, and when another expert must lead the project.

The broader form of engineering creates an important role for IEEE. Its societies already bring together expertise in various technologies, engineering education, technical standards, and other fields. That makes IEEE well placed to help engineers work across specialties without weakening the value of specialization.

IEEE could create more communities organized around problems that require expertise from several fields. Examples include trustworthy clinical AI, resilient infrastructure, energy reliability, scientific discovery, and safe autonomous systems. An engineer could begin in a home discipline and then work with specialists from other IEEE communities as a project requires.

IEEE also can help set practical standards for human-machine collaboration. Engineers will need clear guidance on when AI-generated work must be checked, how uncertainty should be documented, when a specialist must make a decision, and who is responsible when a system uses both human judgment and machine output.

Those questions are becoming part of everyday engineering. They should not be left to each company or project manager to answer independently. A professional organization can provide common expectations that follow engineers as they move between jobs, industries, and technical fields.

AI does not make engineering disciplines less important; it makes the connections between them easier to use. Deep expertise gives engineers the foundation to judge what is sound. Systems thinking helps them understand how different parts of a problem fit together. AI can extend engineers’ ability to explore, test, and communicate across fields. Human judgment gives the work direction and responsibility.

An engineer is not defined only by a job title or a fixed set of tasks. An engineer is someone trained to understand complex systems, define and redefine problems, bring together the knowledge and tools needed to solve them, test whether solutions work, and take responsibility for the outcome.

That is what it means to be an “unbound” engineer.

The boundaries between specialties become easier to cross, and machines might take on more of the technical work, but the core of engineering remains human: deciding what problem is worth solving, what evidence is good enough, how the pieces fit together, and what to do when the answer is uncertain.

Sufian Aldogom is an IEEE member, a research affiliate at MIT, and a senior leader at Google in Sunnyvale, Calif.

#3333. Airbnb can invest in Brian Chesky’s AI lab, its quarterly filing shows

Airbnb’s technology chief holds a stake in Chesky’s AI lab, and independent directors approved the deal. It landed with Airbnb’s fastest revenue growth in three years and a 2027 date for its own AI agent.

Brian Chesky at an Airbnb event in San Francisco in 2018

Brian Chesky’s AI lab paid Airbnb $7.1M for some of its intellectual property and to cover certain expenses, Airbnb disclosed in its quarterly filing on Thursday. Chesky, Airbnb’s chief executive, founded the lab and controls it.

Under the deal, signed this month, Airbnb can choose to join the lab’s future funding rounds. It also gets a licence to use some of the lab’s technology inside its own business. Chief technology officer Ahmad Al-Dahle holds a stake in the lab and works for it too. The Information, which reported the disclosure, said Chesky has funded the lab himself so far, citing a source. TNW has not independently verified that.

“Their roles with the AI Lab do not change their duties and responsibilities to Airbnb,” the filing said of the two executives.

A special committee of independent board members approved the deal under Airbnb’s policy on related-party transactions. The filing does not name the lab or say what it is building.

Al-Dahle joined Airbnb in January from Meta, where he led generative AI, Bloomberg reported at the time. We reported in June that Chesky was building an AI lab of his own.

The filing came with Airbnb’s third-quarter results. Revenue rose 19% to $4.9bn, its fastest growth in more than three years, and net income reached $1.9bn. Nights and seats booked rose 16%. Airbnb now expects revenue to grow in the high teens this year, up from at least the mid-teens. It also approved up to $12bn more in share buybacks.

“It’s rare for a marketplace of our size to reaccelerate growth, but that’s exactly what we’re doing,” Chesky told analysts on Thursday’s earnings call.

Airbnb last raised its forecast in August. Hotels, which it began adding this year, grew “markedly faster” than homes in the quarter, Chesky said.

Shares jumped more than 10% on Friday, Reuters reported. That set Airbnb apart from Booking, Expedia and Tripadvisor. All three have pointed to higher airfares linked to the Iran war and to unrest in parts of Europe, Reuters said.

Airbnb plans to start rolling out its own AI agent for planning and booking trips in the first half of 2027, it said alongside the results. Instead of a chat window, the agent will build each answer from maps, photos, comparisons, calendars and itineraries. It will also handle changes, refunds and payment problems after a booking.

Chesky argued that general assistants such as Meta’s Muse and Instinct are not built for travel. They still send Airbnb little business, he said on the call, as Business Insider reported.

“We’re not seeing a lot of traffic, and even fewer bookings, from Muse and Instinct yet,” Chesky said.

Agent traffic peaked in early October and has not grown since, he added. Airbnb’s own support assistant now resolves about 40% of customer issues without a human. Support costs per booking fell more than 17% from a year earlier, the company said.

#3332. Twelve South’s new Cablesnap charger has a built-in retractable USB-C cable

Popular Apple accessory maker Twelve South is launching a new retractable Cablesnap 65W travel charger this week. It has a built-in USB-C cable, alongside an additional USB-C port and USB-A port.

You can order the new Cablesnap 65W on Amazon today for $49.99.

We’ve seen travel chargers with retractable cables before, and Twelve South’s is similar. It has a 29-inch (75cm) spring-loaded USB-C cable built right in, so you can pull out exactly as much as you need. Then, when you’re ready to pack up, just give it a little pull, and it snaps back into the charging brick.

In addition to the retractable USB-C cable, there’s a separate USB-C port and a USB-A port for charging other accessories. It can charge at up to 65W speeds, shared across each connected device.

You can order the new Cablesnap 65W on Amazon today. This is just the latest in what’s been a busy few weeks for Twelve South. Last month, the accessory maker introduced the popular AirFly Drive adapter that converts wired CarPlay into wireless. A few weeks later it unveiled the AirFly View, an evolution of its wireless audio dongle that’s perfect for planes.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Is there a better time than the weekend to kick back and relax with a nice film? We work all week, and having the chance to kick our feet up and watch a movie is the ultimate way to relax.

This week, I'm locked in on slightly older movies from the Prime Video new releases. We have a late 1980s cartoon that's extremely near and dear to my heart, a Christmas classic and a 2010s goofball movie that'll have you rolling on the floor laughing (assuming you have a tolerance for this sort of oddball humor).

These are the three new-to-Prime Video movies I think you should watch this weekend. There are only so many hours in a weekend, and you don't want to waste a bunch watching a bad film, so we'll guide you to the good ones.

I love "All Dogs Go to Heaven." It's a sad movie — both from a real-world perspective, given the circumstances of young actress Judith Eva Barsi, and from the plot involving the dog Charlie B. Barkin, his best friend Itchy Itchiford, and what happens to dogs when they die. But it's also heartwarming and highly entertaining for people of all ages.

Why is it special to me? As a kid, I went on vacation to Florida, and the day I arrived, I came down with a stomach bug that knocked me out of commission for the entire one-week trip. I literally did nothing but sit around in my grandparents' house for my entire annual vacation. And between trips to the bathroom, I watched "All Dogs Go to Heaven" over and over. You'd think that would make me dislike the movie, since I associate it with a ruined trip, but it brings back happy memories and got me through a difficult week. But it's not nostalgia; I watched it again as an adult with my 9-year-old stepson, and we both loved it.

Watch "All Dogs Go to Heaven" on Prime Video now

This is another throwback to my childhood — I guess I'm in a nostalgic mood today. But instead of associating this with sleeping on the bathroom floor, I remember watching it every winter to get ready for Christmas with the tale of Turbo Man (and sometimes in the middle of summer when I felt like throwing in a funny VHS).

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Starring Arnold Schwarzenegger and Sinbad (yes, unlike the Mandela Effect version of "Shazam," he's really in this one), "Jingle All The Way" follows the hunt for a special toy (the aforementioned Turbo Man) and the chaos of trying to find it on Christmas Eve. Like many kids' movies, it all wraps up with a tidy bow in a completely unrealistic way, but that doesn't make it any less entertaining.

Watch "Jingle All The Way" on Prime Video now

I couldn't put only kid-friendly movies on the list, so the entirely not-child-appropriate "Hot Tub Time Machine" rounds it out. John Cusack, Rob Corddry, Craig Robinson, and Clark Duke contrast each other to create pure hilarity in this raunchy R-rated comedy, where the four go into a hot tub that sends them on a trip through time. It's a goofy premise for a goofy movie.

Keeping today's throwback theme alive, though, is the crew's first destination: 1986, the year I was born. If you remember the 80s fondly and want to see what a group of goofballs from 2010 do in the middle of the decade, you'll love this movie. It even has sci-fi elements that'll scratch fans' itch while keeping them laughing the whole way through.

Watch "Hot Tub Time Machine" on Prime Video starting November 1

#3330. Galiano Gold (GAU) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Mill throughput climbed and costs eased as the Asanko mine's hedge book nears settlement.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Galiano Gold Inc. (GAU +17.93%) reported increased production and strengthened operating cash flow while advancing its long-term life of mine plan at the Asanko Gold Mine. Management stated that the company is on track to meet annual production and cost targets following improved mill performance and higher ore grades from the Abore deposit. The company indicated that the impending completion of its gold hedge program by the end of 2026 will allow for full participation in prevailing gold prices starting in 2027. Strategic focus remains on the development of the Nkran Cut 3 pit and exploration programs aimed at converting mineral resources to reserves.

Operator: Hello, and welcome to the Galiano Gold Third Quarter 2026 Results Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] I will now turn the conference over to Matt Badylak, Galiano's President and Chief Executive Officer.

Matt Badylak: Thank you, operator, and good morning, everyone. We appreciate you taking time to join us on the call today to review Galiano Gold's Third Quarter 2026 financial and operating results, which we released yesterday after market close. During today's call, we'll be making forward-looking statements and referring to non-IFRS performance measures. Please refer to the cautionary notes on Slide 2 of the webcast presentation and to the risk disclosures in our most recent MD&A. Yesterday's news release should be read together with our third quarter financial statements and MD&A, which are available on our website and filed on SEDAR+ and EDGAR. Unless otherwise noted, all dollar amounts discussed on this call are in U.S. dollars.

Joining me today are Michael Cardinaels, our Chief Operating Officer; Matt Freeman, our Chief Financial Officer; and Chris Pettman, our Vice President, Exploration. I will begin with an overview of the quarter. Michael will discuss mining and processing, Matt will review financial performance and costs, and Chris will update you on exploration. I'll then return to discuss near-term priorities and outlook before we open the call for questions. Turning to Slide 4. Q3 demonstrated clear progress across the business. Production increased, cost performance improved and operating cash flow strengthened. Most importantly, we achieved this performance with no recordable injuries. I want to recognize and thank our team and business partners for their discipline and commitment during the quarter.

These results show that we are executing the plan and leave us well positioned to deliver our full year guidance. Our balance sheet remains healthy with no debt, providing the capacity to continue investing in the Asanko Gold Mine. We also continue advancing our long-term priorities. Subsequent to the quarter, we secured extensions to the Abirem and Miradani mining leases. This important milestone provides greater operating certainty and supports the execution of our current life of mine plan. We appreciate the support of the Government of Ghana and the positive engagement of the Minerals Commission and the Ministry of Lands and Natural Resources throughout this process.

During the quarter, we also advanced key initiatives at Nkran Cut 3, Esaase and Abore. The key message from Q3 is that the operating performance is strengthening while our longer-term initiatives continue to advance. We entered the final quarter with confidence in our ability to deliver our 2026 plan. With that, I'll turn the call over to Michael to review operating performance.

Michael Cardinaels: Thank you, Matt, and good morning, everyone. Q3 marked a step forward operationally. As Matt noted, we delivered these results while maintaining our strong safety record. At September 30, our team had worked approximately 13.4 million hours without a lost time injury and achieved 548 consecutive injury-free days. Following another safe production quarter, both our lost time injury frequency rate and total recordable injury frequency rate now stand at 0, which is an achievement worth celebrating. Here on Slide 5, mining activity advanced in line with our 2026 plan. We mined 1.7 million tonnes of ore at an average grade of 1 gram per tonne, with a strip ratio of 4.4:1.

Abore remained our primary ore source, accounting for roughly 82% of the Q3 total mined ore, contributing 1.4 million tonnes at an average grade of 1.1 grams per tonne. Grades rose 9% from Q2 as mining moved into deeper elevations consistent with our mine plan. Esaase supplemented this supply with 0.3 million tonnes at an average grade of 0.8 grams per tonne. Development at Nkran Cut 3 also accelerated. Additional equipment mobilized in Q3 helped lift development waste movement by a further 40% to 8.5 million tonnes. We invested $24.6 million in pre-stripping, bringing the year-to-date total to $60.2 million. We expect mining rates to remain steady in Q4 as the program progresses according to schedule. Turning to Slide 6.

Stronger plant performance was a key driver of production growth. Availability reached 93%, enabling us to mill 1.4 million tonnes, 11% more than in Q2. Mill feed grade rose 11% to an average of 1 gram per tonne, reflecting the planned benefit of higher ore grades in the second half of the year. Recovery held steady at 90% and the combination of greater throughput, higher feed grades and stable recovery resulted in production of 40,922 ounces, up 19% from Q2. With just over 110,000 ounces produced through the first 9 months of the year, we enter Q4 with solid operating momentum from an improved Q3 and remain confident in achieving our full year production guidance.

Our focus is to sustain safe, reliable execution across the mine and the processing plant and close out the year strongly. I will now hand the call over to Matt Freeman to review financial results.

Matthew Freeman: Thanks, Michael. Good morning, everyone. Turning to Slide 7. Stronger production and gold sales in the third quarter translated into a meaningful improvement in our financial performance and cash generation. Revenue for the quarter was $172 million on sales of just over 40,000 ounces of gold at an average realized price of $4,247 per ounce before the impact of hedges. This translated into strong financial results with adjusted EBITDA of $93.3 million, basic EPS of $0.15 and adjusted EPS of $0.09. The business also generated $57 million of operating cash flow during the quarter compared with $40 million in Q3 of 2025.

The increase was driven by higher gold prices and more ounces sold, partly offset by higher royalties and the income taxes we have to pay. The most significant change from 1 year ago was net income, we reported -- net income attributable to our shareholders of $40 million compared to the net loss last year of $39 million, representing a positive swing of $79 million. The improvement was mainly driven by higher revenues, again, reflecting more ounces sold and higher gold prices, offset, as I mentioned before, by royalties. Also, as we have discussed previously, we're now very close to the end of our hedge program.

We settled 22,500 ounces during the quarter, leaving only 15,000 ounces to be settled in Q4. Once those remaining ounces are delivered, the hedge program will be complete, enabling our financial results to fully participate in the gold price beginning in 2027. Our financial position at September 30 remains very strong with $87 million of cash with the $75 million revolving credit facility remaining undrawn. The key point is that our balance sheet remains very healthy, maintaining substantial liquidity to fund Nkran Cut 3, our exploration programs and other growth priorities. Turning to Slide 8. We're also pleased to see all-in sustaining costs improve to $2,346 per ounce for the quarter, a 5% improvement from Q2.

The primary driver of this improvement was the higher gold ounces sold, partly offset by increasing sustaining capital related to the expansion of the tailings storage facility. Year-to-date, AISC was $2,391 per ounce within the bottom half of our annual guidance range, such that our 2026 AISC guidance remains unchanged between $2,300 and $2,600 per ounce. The disciplined approach to cost management allows us to continue directing capital towards value-enhancing projects, including Nkran Cut 3 and our exploration programs at Esaase and Abore, which will support future production and the potential for mine life extension. With that, I will now turn the call over to Chris to discuss the exploration progress.

Chris Pettman: Thanks, Matt. Turning to Slide 9. Our exploration work through Q3 remained focused on advancing reserve conversion at Esaase and underground resource growth at Abore with both programs supporting our planned mineral resource and mineral reserve update in the first quarter of 2027. At Esaase, we achieved an important milestone by completing the expanded infill drilling program during the quarter. We drilled 16,732 meters in Q3, bringing the total program to 32,982 meters completed. The program was designed to convert existing open pit mineral resources from the inferred to the indicated category and has the potential to significantly increase the Esaase mineral reserve and support planning for a potential future open pit expansion. Data review and modelling are now underway.

At Abore, drilling resumed in late Q3 after the program was paused to prioritize the completion of the Esaase campaign. We drilled 4,445 meters during the quarter, bringing year-to-date drilling to approximately 20,600 meters of the planned 32,000-meter program. This work is designed to expand the underground mineral resource through step-out drilling outside of the existing resource. We expect to complete this work in the remainder of the program in Q4. We also achieved a significant milestone by receiving all regulatory approvals required for construction of the planned Abore exploration adit. This is an exciting moment for us as the adit will provide a more efficient platform for underground drilling and support further evaluation of Abore's longer-term underground potential.

This is the culmination of 3 years of successful surface exploration programs at Abore and marks what may be a defining moment for the AGM and the deposits of the Asanko belt. I'd like to personally thank and congratulate all of the members of the AGM site exploration team for their hard work and technical excellence that has brought us to this point. Back to you, Matt, to discuss our priorities and outlook.

Matt Badylak: Thank you, Chris. Before we turn to questions, let me leave you with one clear takeaway. Q3 showed that this team can deliver. We strengthened our operational and financial performance, advanced our long-term plan and maintained a strong safety record. Through the first 9 months, we have positioned the business to finish the year safely and deliver our full year production and cost guidance. That is our immediate priority. Beyond the year-end, the opportunity is equally clear. The completion of the hedge book, together with higher production should drive strong operating cash flow in 2027. We will remain disciplined in allocating capital, continuing to invest in the business and advancing growth opportunities that can create long-term value for shareholders.

We have the team, the assets and the financial strength to deliver our plan, and we remain confident in our path ahead. Operator, we are now ready to take questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your first question today comes from the line of Jeremy Hoy from Canaccord Genuity.

Jeremy Hoy: I guess first question for me is on 2027. Any color you guys can provide on the various cost components heading into the new year might be helpful as we look at our estimates for the following year.

Matt Badylak: Jeremy, thanks for your question. Yes, obviously, we're working through all of those numbers at the moment internally, and we will be looking to provide the market with clarity on what 2027 looks like in normal cadence early in 2027. So yes, I just request patience on that at the moment as the team works through that. But obviously, we have previously suggested that we are expecting slightly higher production in 2027 on the back of higher grades, et cetera. And we're looking forward to, as we said, those mineral reserves and resource updates that the team is working through at the moment, which will help drive those numbers and solidify those numbers in due course.

Jeremy Hoy: Okay. And with costs and upward pressure on fuel prices being topical through the sector. Could you remind us the hedging strategy for fuel and other inputs?

Matthew Freeman: Jeremy, it's Matt Freeman here. Yes, we're looking at those things. I mean obviously, at the moment, with diesel pricing elevated because of the conflict in the Middle East, we're kind of being careful on that. But we keep an eye on it quarter-by-quarter, and we'll react if we need to, if we feel the need. At the moment, I mean, although there's an increase in diesel price, it's -- we still feel comfortable with our cost structure. And as we said, we're coming at the low end of our production -- our cost guidance range for the year. So we're comfortable with where we are at the moment.

Jeremy Hoy: Okay. Great. Much appreciated. Last one for me is I guess on the underground opportunity. Great to see you get the approvals for the adit and will be good to see drills get in there and attack that ground from a better vantage point. Could you run us through any updated thinking on timing of how that underground opportunity progresses? It's exciting because it's upside potential to what we're modeling on an open pit basis only. So anything that you could provide would be very helpful.

Matt Badylak: Yes. Jeremy, that's a good question. I would like to just highlight Chris and the team's work on advancing that expeditiously in the last quarter. We have advanced quite healthily through the tender process during the quarter, and we are looking to kind of finalize that process, which would include selection of a mining contractor within the quarter, and that will then allow that selected contractor to get going with equipment mobilization, et cetera, and start to look to break ground as soon as possible, right? So I think we've previously discussed that we're looking to try and do that by Q1 or late Q1, early Q2 next year in terms of the groundbreaking.

But obviously, that will depend on the contractor selection, et cetera, which that process is currently underway. And then the adit itself is -- we're looking at about a 2-kilometer adit as well and drilling will obviously take place as we progress that forward. Chris, I'm not sure if you want to add anything to that.

Chris Pettman: No, I think that's a pretty good overall overview, Matt. I think that in terms of when we can actually drill underground, I guess the one thing I would add is that we're not going to wait until we get to the bottom and do all the drilling. We will be able to drill some of our areas as we progress the ramp. So it won't be the full sort of 1.5 years of construction before we start to see some drill results come out of that.

Jeremy Hoy: That's great. And any idea when you might look at an initial underground study? Or is it just too early to say?

Matt Badylak: Yes. I mean I think, obviously, we're going to have to do a fair bit of drilling from underground and do some conversion first. Obviously, we have last year -- or sorry, earlier this year, we've updated MRE with a maiden underground mineral resource at both Abore and Nkran. There's a bit of drilling, obviously, that needs to be done before we can get going on a comprehensive study. So that's still some time away at this stage. But obviously, we've got the cash, Jeremy, to be able to advance this project as quickly as possible, and that's the intention and then to define what it is that an underground ultimately looks like as soon as we possibly can.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your next question comes from the line of Bereket Berhe from Beacon Securities.

Bereket Berhe: Congratulations. It looks like we have approached or we are at the inflection point here. And hopefully, this is only the beginning of the good stuff. You may not need Esaase unless mining slows down for whatever reason. What would your thinking be around that?

Matt Badylak: Okay. I'll start off with your first question, and then I'll pass on to Mick for the second. Yes, as I mentioned before, Bereket, we are close to finalizing the tender process at the moment. So I don't want to step ahead of that at the moment with regards to giving you guidance on cost. But just suffice to say that once we do have that process behind us, we will be able to update the market on the costs around that adit, which isn't too far away again and provide you with clarity on that.

So again, just requesting a slight amount of patience from your end on that side, but we will provide you with details as soon as we have finalized numbers available to us. Go ahead, Mick.

Michael Cardinaels: Very good. In terms of the production and the mill feed strategy, as everyone is well aware, the material that we get from Abore is extremely hard. It's harder than the rest of our deposits. So there is a fine line between throughput and grade that we manage on a daily basis and a shift-by-shift basis. So the feed blending strategy will continue around 80% to 85% from Abore based on available material and grade. Bereket Berhe: And if I can add a question, what would the visible grade profile of Abore look from here to, say, Q1 and Q2?

And then as I mentioned earlier, the full year guidance is probably what you're really looking for, and that's going to come out in early February in Q1 there. Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Heiko Ihle from H.C. Wainwright.

Heiko Ihle: Can you give a bit of color on what you see with labor costs for next year? Maybe just a bit on like headcount and cost per worker, obviously, with the Nkran Cut 3.

We're fully equipped, fully staffed and ready to go. The Nkran Cut 3, as you know, it's contract mined, that's all on contract rates and contract volumes. So again, I don't think you should see any surprises there as we move into next year.

It's really a volume-based exercise at Nkran Cut 3.

Heiko Ihle: How many people are on the payroll right now at site?

Matthew Freeman: Well, I think as you know, we have a modest employee base, and then we have a large number of contractors on site with our 2 main mining contractors at Rabotec at Esaase and Rocksure at Nkran, who actually make more -- there's more of those employees, their employees than our own. We're around 450 of the Asanko employees and then the rest of the cohort add up to more than a couple of thousand people in total.

Heiko Ihle: Okay. And then just one final one. With Nkran Cut 3, the mining costs obviously decreased. Can you give a bit of color on not even just like short term, but intermediate and longer-term factors that we should use to analyze our estimates for mining costs in the out years?

Matthew Freeman: Yes. I think the best way to look at that is the good thing is we're locked into long-term mining contracts here. So we're not expecting any particular change to the cost structure. What you're seeing the benefit with Nkran Cut 3 as we start to increase the volumes, our fixed management charges obviously come down on a unit basis. So the more tonnes we can move each month, the lower cost per tonne effectively comes in. So from that perspective, that's where you start to see it drop in Q3. And as Mick has alluded to, we're sort of increasing to add a bit more equipment to site.

So as we accelerate through the Nkran strip, so we should see hopefully flat or positive trends in those costs. Obviously, there's some underlying inflation of diesel and other things. But broadly, the contracts are fairly well set for the next number of years. So I think you can be very confident modeling consistent run rates what we've seen.

#3329. Consumer Appetite for Personal AI Goes Mainstream

Nearly 70 percent of respondents say they want an AI assistant in their next device, according to a new report

Qualcomm builds intelligent, connected, computing and AI solutions that transform industries and advance human progress.

A recent report by Qualcomm Technologies, built on a survey of more than 12,000 people across key geographies worldwide, shows that around 70 percent of respondents express strong interest in an AI assistant that can interact naturally through voice and seamlessly manage devices, apps, and everyday tasks.

This article is brought to you by Qualcomm Technologies.

For many consumers, much of the promise and appeal of AI is personal. Consumers are looking past generic tools and want to know how these technologies will help them in their daily lives. These trends coincide with the advent of new classes of wearable devices that, in addition to being able to leverage powerful frontier models, feature built-in intelligence that understand the context of a user. Where are they? What are they seeing and hearing? What are their habits, their preferences, their schedules?

It’s an astonishing pivot, from passive accessories that served mostly to send users smartphone notifications to proactive, intelligent companions. The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI. And it shifts the focus toward you, the user.

These new technologies are exciting. But what do consumers really want?

A Personal AI report, commissioned by Qualcomm Technologies, built on a survey of more than 12,000 people across key geographies worldwide (the U.S., U.K., Germany, India, Brazil, and China) focused on the rise of personal AI in intelligent wearables looks deeply at these developments.

The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI.

Survey respondents are less interested in single devices and are responding more to the idea of connected ecosystems. As people expand their roster of devices, it only makes sense. Instead of relying entirely on a smartphone and a laptop, respondents also have connected technology in their cars, as well as intelligent wearables like smartwatches, smart glasses, hearables, and other wearables like rings, pins, and pendants. They want those devices to work in concert, and the way to do that is to decentralize any single one of them. Instead, the AI agent that knows the user and works across all of those devices becomes the unifying factor.

Consider a typical workday: A user’s watch detects it is time to leave for a meeting and, with permission, their AI agent factors in calendar details, real-time traffic and battery status across their devices. In the car, it suggests the best route and briefs them on their meeting agenda. As they arrive, smart glasses surface a discreet reminder, such as the meeting location or the name of a new contact, while the phone stays in their pocket. No one device has to do everything; each plays the role it is best suited for, coordinated by a personal AI agent that understands the user’s context and acts only at the user’s direction.

With this in mind, simply adding more hardware to the mix isn’t sufficient. Even though respondents will be open to new form factors, they’ll demand more from their ecosystem of devices. They’ll be sensitive to points of friction and needless complexity, and they’ll require each new device to bring something new to the table — “incremental intelligence, convenience, or contextual awareness that their existing devices cannot deliver on their own what the report,” reads the report.

The usage trends are up. The report found that those who own wearables are already using AI frequently (60 percent use it at least weekly), which indicates that it’s becoming less of a fun experiment for early adopters and more of a critical mass habit.

The “always-on” nature of intelligent wearables appears to be winning respondents, too. The report found the following statistics on average continuous wear among users:

But for all the excitement and engagement around intelligent wearables, there’s a gating factor: trust. As use cases for intelligent wearables expands to more personal and persistent experiences, trust is a necessity for Personal AI.

Notably, the report found that respondents expressed more interest in adopting intelligent wearables when Snapdragon was introduced as the enabling platform. This reinforces the value of having an established, trusted technology foundation in the mix.

The report shows that consumer appetite for AI is high, with 60-70 percent of those surveyed expressing interest in advanced AI as they consider a new device. That’s a constant. But remaining purchase drivers differed between device categories.

Audio playback quality is the most influential purchase driver for true wireless earbuds and headphones. For smartwatches, it’s display quality and responsiveness. Respondents are less concerned about technical specifications than aesthetics like materials and finish when it comes to devices like smart rings and pendants. And for smart glasses, it’s all about the type of control, whether it’s voice, gesture, or touch.

Artificial intelligence is entering a new phase, one that is deeply personal, continuously present, and seamlessly embedded into the devices we wear every day. This evolution, which we define as “Personal AI”, represents a shift away from generic, cloud-only intelligence toward AI that understands individuals in context: their habits, preferences, environments, and intent, in real time.

Alongside these purchase drivers is another key finding: Consumer appetite for Personal AI agents has gone mainstream. The report says that 70 percent of respondents “express strong interest in an AI assistant that can interact naturally through voice and seamlessly manage devices, apps, and everyday tasks.” With each individual as the center of their own ecosystem, voice becomes the most critical, natural method for interacting with agents.

Intelligent wearables comprise much of the hardware of this “ecosystem of you.” Consumers are interested in ecosystems instead of single devices, and they’re looking for agentic AI capabilities that understand and act on their behalf.

Yet so much of the industry remains undefined. OEMs and technology makers have an enormous opportunity right now to innovate and iterate on the strong technological foundations that platform makers are building. And the roadmap for what consumers want is clear.

All percentages, consumer behaviors, and attitudes stated in this report are based only on the responses of the individuals who participated in our survey.

Qualcomm Technologies is a global leader in communications and computing technologies, including leading-edge AI, high-performance, low-power computing, and connectivity solutions. Headquartered in San Diego, Calif., the company develops technologies for next-generation mobile networks and smart devices, and designs semiconductors such as mobile processors and AI chips.

The bias is deafening. Qualcomm, a chip manufacturer that is all in on AI, makes a survey and then states they found everyone loves using AI, the very AI that will run on Qualcomm chips. Clearly they don't have a conflict of interest in this. /s

#3328. Tesla to wind down Cybertruck production in mid-2027 to build Cybercabs

Elon Musk made the announcement on X, after sales fell far below the 250,000 a year he once predicted.

Tesla will stop making most Cybertrucks at its Texas factory around the middle of next year, chief executive Elon Musk said on Friday. The space will instead be used to build more Cybercabs, the company’s two-seat robotaxis.

Musk announced the plan in a post on X, but he did not say whether production would end completely.

Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production

Gigafactory Texas is the only plant that builds the Cybertruck. Tesla has not said what will happen to parts and servicing for existing owners. The truck has sold far below Tesla’s early hopes.

In 2023, Musk said Tesla could eventually sell 250,000 to 500,000 a year. However, the company has sold only tens of thousands in total since deliveries began in late 2023.

Tesla does not report Cybertruck sales on their own. Instead, it groups them with the Model S, Model X, and Semi, and that category fell 48% from a year earlier to 8,295 vehicles in the third quarter.

Based on those figures, Electrek estimates Tesla has delivered about 70,000 Cybertrucks in three years. The truck also missed the goals Tesla set when it was unveiled in 2019.

Also, the company promised a price under $40,000 and a range of up to 500 miles, but the truck arrived two years late, at about $60,000 and with a shorter range. Today the cheapest version starts at $74,990, after a $5,000 price rise in August.

Its divisive design and high price weighed on sales. Musk’s political activity in 2024 and 2025 also made the truck a target for protests, TechCrunch reported.

The Cybertruck is the latest product Tesla has dropped as it puts more money into AI and robotics. Earlier this year, it ended production of the Model S and Model X and used that space to build Optimus humanoid robots.

Meanwhile, Cybercab has been carrying passengers in Austin for about two months. Tesla plans to expand the service to Dallas later this month.

#3325. Multiphysics Modeling for Next-Generation Electromagnetic Manufacturing Technologies



Advances in sensing, manufacturing, computational resources, and data-driven methods are enabling new approaches to electromagnetic sensing, non-destructive evaluation, and advanced materials processing. This webinar will demonstrate how the COMSOL Multiphysics software supports predictive modeling by coupling electromagnetic fields with thermal, chemical, mechanical, and transport phenomena across multiple length and time scales.

The first application we will show focuses on eddy-current thermometry for reconstructing three-dimensional temperature fields in metal plates. Temperature-dependent electrical conductivity alters induced currents and magnetic fields, enabling volumetric thermal inference. COMSOL simulations of defects and laser-induced transient heating will support validation of reconstruction algorithms. Multifrequency excitation will be investigated to improve depth discrimination through frequency-dependent penetration depths and sensitivities.

The second application examines microwave-enabled volumetric additive manufacturing of ceramic components. A high-power microwave beamforming array delivers localized energy into three-dimensional volumes, enabling processing of opaque, particle-laden resins. Coupled COMSOL models of electromagnetic propagation, microwave absorption, heat transfer, and ceramic sintering kinetics are used to predict temperature evolution, reaction progression, spatial resolution, and processing scalability. Future extensions will incorporate pulsed excitation, fluid flow, resin viscosity, convection, shrinkage, and solid mechanics.

Together, these examples demonstrate how the COMSOL software can integrate multiphysics modeling with sensing, manufacturing, and data inversion. This webinar will present two applications of coupled electromagnetic and thermal modeling in COMSOL Multiphysics: eddy-current thermometry in metal plates and microwave-assisted processing of ceramic-loaded resins. By connecting simulation with practical engineering systems, COMSOL-based modeling can accelerate technology development, reduce experimental iteration, and support reliable scale-up of next-generation electromagnetic technologies.

#3324. Fox completes $22bn Roku acquisition and puts it in a new digital unit

This article was published on June 15, 2026 GMT

The deal closed today, and Roku now sits in a new division with Tubi and Fox One.

Fox Corporation has completed its acquisition of Roku, the maker of streaming sticks and smart TV software, in a cash-and-stock deal worth about $22bn. The deal closed on Friday, and Roku’s shares stopped trading on Nasdaq the same day.

Fox agreed to buy Roku in June and had expected to close in the first half of 2027. The deal gives it direct access to more than 100 million households that use Roku devices.

Under the final terms, Roku shareholders receive $95.30 in cash and 0.9799 Fox Class A shares for each share. In June, the companies had announced $96 in cash and 0.9693 Fox shares. Former Roku shareholders now own about 26% of Fox.

Roku joins a new division, Fox Digital Platforms, together with the free streaming service Tubi, the Fox One app, and podcast company Red Seat Ventures.

Founder Anthony Wood joins Fox’s board and becomes co-chair of the division, while Paul Cheesbrough is its co-chair and chief executive.

“We started Roku more than two decades ago to give people a better way to watch TV, and that mission doesn’t change today,” Wood said.

For Fox, the value lies in Roku’s platform rather than its devices. Roku reaches more than half of all US broadband homes, and its platform business made $4.1bn last year, 87.5% of its revenue, mostly from advertising and deals with streaming services.

As a result, Fox now owns a connected-TV advertising business, data on what viewers watch and a home screen where it can promote its own sports, news and Tubi.

However, that home screen also carries rivals such as Netflix and Disney. Fox has promised to keep Roku open to all partners, and it expects the deal to save about $400m a year in costs within two years.

The deal is part of a wave of media consolidation. Days before it was announced, the US Justice Department cleared Paramount’s purchase of Warner Bros. Discovery.

Aside from the best foldable phones, I tend to see a lot of innovation around rugged phones built for long-term off-grid living or weekend camping getaways.

I’ve tested my fair share of unconventional ones: from the projector-packing Blackview Xplore 2 all the way to the Sonim XP Pro Thermal with its Predator-like heat vision. Every single one brought something wild to the table, but the Oukitel WP63 packs something I genuinely haven't seen before: a built-in electronic fire igniter.

While most phone manufacturers design their hardware specifically to avoid catching fire (ahem, Note 7), this heavy-duty slab embraces it for emergency survival. Honestly, it’s one of the most interesting rugged phones I’ve come across this year.

If the igniter alone isn’t enough to convince you, it also packs a massive 20,000mAh battery, a built-in reverse-charging cable, an all-in-one camping lantern, and a night vision camera.

Best of all, it’s currently 43% off for a limited time, dropping the price from $599 down to $339.

Built for extreme off-grid adventures, the Oukitel WP63 features an emergency electronic fire igniter, massive 20,000 mAh battery, built-in reverse-charging cable, 6.67-inch 120Hz display, rear camping lantern, and an 8MP night vision camera to see through the darkness.

The integrated lighter on the Oukitel WP63 brings back memories of the push-in cigarette lighters found in old-school cars. The heating element is tucked away on the top edge of the phone, popping open to reveal the recessed coil with a light press. Through the dedicated Lighter app, I can trigger the ignition process, which quickly causes the coil to glow with that familiar cherry-red warmth.

It generates concentrated heat capable of sparking dry materials on direct contact — like scrap paper or dried-up leaves that have been baking under the sun. For safety reasons, the igniter enforces an automatic cooldown period of around 10 seconds to prevent the housing from overheating.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

While I was genuinely surprised by how easily it lit the corner of an envelope, keep in mind that nursing that spark into a sustainable fire takes real effort. Because it doesn’t produce an open flame like a Bic lighter or butane torch, having prior campfire-building experience makes a huge difference. After several tries, I managed to get a small bundle of brittle autumn leaves to catch, but it definitely requires patience and bone-dry kindling.

Beyond its standard 64MP main shooter — which delivers respectable shots when lighting conditions cooperate — Oukitel also throws in a dedicated 8MP infrared night vision camera. For a rugged phone built for the backcountry, it’s an invaluable tool the moment true darkness sets in.

While dedicated night vision cameras I’ve tested offer superior performance, especially in how far their IR illuminators can reach, the WP63’s sensor is still ideal for scanning your immediate vicinity for critters rustling in the brush. If you're out camping, it's especially handy when you have to step out of your tent half-asleep in the dead of night and your eyes haven't yet adjusted to the blackness.

Even though the setup is limited to just a single main camera and a night vision lens, the quality from the primary sensor more than suffices for the quick run-and-gun shots I want to share on social media. And the selfie camera up front isn’t too shabby, either.

As much as I rely on the flashlight on my phones, they’re dinky compared to the blinding beam produced by the WP63’s rear-mounted camping light. At its brightest, it effortlessly illuminates an entire pitch-dark area, and it has serious endurance thanks to the massive 20,000 mAh battery packed inside. With hurricane season in full swing, I’m confident it could easily hold up through an extended power outage. On top of that, an emergency strobe function unleashes an intense beacon that can be spotted from long distances.

I also want to highlight the 3W loudspeaker mounted on the back, which completely puts flagship phone audio to shame. While most phones tend to distort heavily at maximum volume, this speaker delivers surprising low-end punch and clarity — making it feel like I’m carrying a dedicated Bluetooth speaker in my pocket.

The Oukitel WP63 is an unlocked phone ready to run on virtually any wireless carrier, and I love that it features one of the easiest SIM card slots to access without hunting down an ejector pin.

This Swiss Army knife approach works because it nails the practical essentials for off the grid excursions — headlined by its halo feature, the built-in igniter. That utility is backed by smart additions like an integrated USB-C cable, allowing it to double as a ready-to-go power bank for other gear.

Tipping the scales at over 1.3 pounds, it’s certainly not a device I’d want as my primary everyday carry. But as a secondary backup? It’s an easy sell, especially while it's 43% off. Whether you toss it into a glove compartment for road trips or pack it along for a weekend in the woods, the Oukitel WP63 delivers rugged peace of mind when facing worst-case scenarios.

#3320. When Electric Cars Were for Women

Early carmakers decided women wanted cars that were quiet, clean, and easy to start

Allison Marsh is a professor at the University of South Carolina and the codirector of the Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society.

When automobiles were still a novelty, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion.

At the turn of the last century, the automobile industry was still new and evolving rapidly. In 1898, there were about 50 carmakers in the United States. A decade later, that number had increased fivefold. In 1901, the companies produced 7,000 vehicles. By 1910, production had reached 181,000.

For several decades, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion, and nobody was sure which technology would come out on top. Steam had the legacy of locomotive technology behind it but came with a risk of fire. Steam-powered vehicles could also become exceedingly hot, depending on the placement of the boiler and the steam piping. Both gasoline and electric cars faced logistical challenges: How far could you travel without refueling or charging? You could always throw an extra can of gasoline in the back of the car, but charging a battery involved more planning. The infrastructure for long-distance travel was not yet in place.

Before the invention of the electric starter in 1911, gasoline-powered engines had to be started with a hand crank; once running, they were loud and emitted noxious fumes. Fully electric vehicles, by contrast, were easy to start; you just turned on the main battery switch, often with a key, and there was no foul exhaust to deal with.

Electric carmakers looking for a way to differentiate their products decided that these attributes made their vehicles perfect for women. (Electric cars were also marketed to doctors so that they could make house calls in the middle of the night without waking the neighbors.) General Electric, which made car chargers based on mercury-arc rectifiers, was so captivated by the idea of women driving electric cars that the company created a series of advertisements featuring stylishly dressed women plugging in their cars and posing with their charging stations.

In ads for its electric car chargers, General Electric featured women using the equipment.miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

A young woman named Fannie Goodnow was an early EV adopter. She owned a 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton, an open two-seater that really did look like a horseless carriage, and she used a GE mercury-arc rectifier to charge it.

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt invented the mercury vapor lamp, which became the basis for the mercury-arc rectifier used in car-charging systems. Bettmann/Getty Images

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt is generally credited with the invention of the mercury-arc rectifier. During the first decade of the 20th century, Hewitt received several U.S. patents for electric lamps and other apparatus for transmitting and using electric currents. U.S. patents 968,896 and 1,163,706, granted to Percy H. Thomas, advanced Hewitt’s designs. Thomas was chief electrician for the Cooper Hewitt Electric Co., which Hewitt had cofounded with George Westinghouse to manufacture and sell his lamps.

The mercury-arc rectifier functioned as a diode. In a car charger like the one Fannie Goodnow used, it converted alternating current from the power grid into direct current needed to charge the car’s battery. A small amount of liquid mercury contained in a glass tube would vaporize and glow as electricity passed through it. Coupled with the carbon anodes, the vapor allowed current to flow in only one direction. This unit took about 12 hours to charge a drained battery.

I couldn’t find any records as to why Fannie Goodnow opted for an electric car. But as a well-to-do woman living in the Boston area, she had more than a half dozen automobile producers to choose from. The one she chose was S.R. Bailey & Co. of Amesbury, Mass.

This early electric car charger used a mercury-arc rectifier to convert AC to DC.Heritage Museums & Gardens

According to Galen Handy, who maintains the Early Electric Vehicles website, Samuel Robinson Bailey started in the carriage and sleigh business as a teenager, winning a best-in-show prize at a carriage exhibition in Portland, Maine, in 1855. Bailey developed a reputation as an inventor and designed processes to streamline the manufacture of his vehicles. He went into business for himself in 1882. Just over a decade later, one of Bailey’s carriages won a gold medal at the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago.

Bailey’s son Edwin attended the exposition, where he likely would have seen a vision of the future: the Morrison electric wagon. This six-passenger, battery-powered vehicle ferried visitors and VIPs around the fairgrounds. It wasn’t long before automobiles began eating into the carriage business. In December 1906, with the carriage industry collapsing, S.R. Bailey & Co. announced it was getting into electric vehicles.

Bailey’s first model, the Victoria Phaeton, used an Edison alkaline battery. Thomas Edison had been working on a lighter, more reliable, and more powerful battery for the auto industry since the 1890s, and announced the achievement with great fanfare in 1903. Unfortunately for Bailey and other carmakers who deployed it, the battery leaked and wouldn’t hold a charge. Edison was forced to go back to the drawing board. By 1910, he had a better battery in production, but by then his friend Henry Ford had introduced the Model T, setting the stage for the internal combustion engine to take over the market.

While Edison toiled to improve his tech, Bailey pivoted to a battery from the Gould Storage Battery Co. of Depew, N.Y. Gould also supplied batteries for railroads, utilities, subways, elevators, and farms. Goodnow’s Victoria Phaeton used a 30-cell lead-acid battery housed in a wooden box that was suspended under the chassis. The standard battery had a range of 64 to 80 kilometers; a larger battery with 50 percent more capacity was available for an upcharge. With the standard battery, the Victoria Phaeton cost US $2,000 (about $73,000 today, or about the list price of an upscale EV like the Audi Q8 or BMW i5).

Fannie Goodnow’s electric car charger now resides at the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. But her 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton has been lost to history. Shown here is a 1911 version of that model.Sarah Thornington/Heritage Museums & Gardens

Goodnow installed a mercury-arc rectifier charging station in the barn adjacent to her parents’ summer home in Hull, Mass. Bill Lillie of Vintage Electric Cars notes that the charging plug was of an unusual design. This is, of course, one of the banes of any early adopter: nonstandardized plugs and cables. The Electric Vehicle Association of America, which formed in 1910, tried to put forward a standard so that electric vehicles could be charged at any charging station. (Modern EV owners can no doubt relate.) But savvy electric car owners knew to carry spare plug adapters and cables when traveling.

When Edison’s improved battery was finally available, Bailey began using it in the Victoria Phaeton and then went on a publicity blitz. In September 1910, the carmaker sponsored a round-trip tour from New York to Boston, with a side trip up New Hampshire’s Mount Washington, totaling about 1,600 km. Sadly, the “This Car Climbed Mt. Washington” bumper sticker hadn’t yet become popular.

Thomas Edison supplied the batteries for an electric car made by S.R. Bailey & Co., which then went on a publicity road trip from New York to Boston. miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

Although Thomas Edison posed for a photo with the new Bailey Victoria Phaeton that featured his new battery, he himself chose a Detroit Electric Victoria for his own use. (Edison was known to be a terrible driver, so someone else likely chauffeured him around.)

Unable to compete against the rising tide of Model Ts, S.R. Bailey sold its factory in 1915, having produced about 500 to 600 electric vehicles.

Although the vehicle Fannie Goodnow chose turned out to be just a blip in automotive history, I like to imagine her driving about town in a beautiful car that embodied all the quirks of early adoption. I hope her friends didn’t make fun of her for investing in electric just before internal combustion took off. I hope she didn’t get stranded without the proper charging cable. I do not know what happened to her or her Victoria Phaeton, but her charging station remained in situ until 2022, when it was donated to the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. Now it stands ready to tell stories of technological change and adoption that continue to resonate today.

Part of a continuing series looking at historical artifacts that embrace the boundless potential of technology.

An abridged version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue.

References For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.

Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

Allison Marsh is a professor in Women and Gender Studies at the University of South Carolina and codirector of the university’s Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society. She combines her interests in engineering, history, and museum objects to write the Past Forward column, which tells the story of technology through historical artifacts. Marsh is currently working on a book on the history of women in electrical engineering.

#3319. Amazon’s Alexa for Shopping agent will now take your orders by text

The AI agent searches, compares and buys for invited US customers, with sponsored products in the replies.

A text conversation with Alexa for Shopping, which adds lasagna ingredients to an Amazon cart, in an example from Amazon.

Amazon is rolling out texting for Alexa for Shopping, its AI shopping agent, starting with invited US customers. It can find products, place orders and track prices by text. Sponsored products can show up in its replies, free to advertisers for now.

Amazon is letting shoppers text its AI shopping agent, Alexa for Shopping, which can search for products, compare them and place orders for them, the company said on Friday. The feature is starting with a small group of invited US customers, with millions more to get access in the coming weeks.

Customers who opt in get a contact called “Alexa Shopping.” They can text a request, such as needing more dog food, or send a photo of a recipe or an outfit, and the agent texts back with options. It buys with the customer’s approval, or automatically when a price hits a target they set.

It can also track price drops, reorder past purchases and check on packages. Amazon says a conversation started by text will carry over to its app, website and Alexa devices.

“Now with Alexa for Shopping, your personal shopping agent is just a text away,” said Rajiv Mehta, Amazon’s vice president of conversational shopping.

The text thread is also a new place for ads. Sponsored products can appear among the options the agent sends, though Amazon is not charging advertisers yet, and purchases the agent completes on its own carry no ads, Digiday reported. Amazon made more than $68B from advertising in 2025.

Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping in May and says more than 400 million customers used it in the past year. In September, it blocked Meta’s Muse agent from shopping its site. Last week, chief executive Andy Jassy said he expects Alexa for Shopping to become the main agent people use to buy from Amazon.

Rivals are moving into messaging too. OpenAI added texting to Dot, its personal agent, last month, and DoorDash began taking orders by text in September, GeekWire reported.

#3318. Apple says there are already over 100,000 apps built for iPhone Duo

Apple released the iPhone Duo two weeks ago, and the app story is quickly taking shape. In a new statement to 9to5Mac, Apple has revealed that there are already “well over 100,000 apps” on the App Store designed for iPhone Duo, and thousands are being added each day.

Here’s Susan Prescott, Apple’s vice president of Worldwide Developer Relations:

“It’s been wonderful to see how quickly developers have embraced iPhone Duo, and we’re grateful for their creativity and innovation. Today there are well over 100,000 apps built for iPhone Duo already live on the App Store, and thousands of optimized apps are being added to the store each day.

“In the last month alone, thousands of developers have joined us for workshops in 19 cities around the world to experience iPhone Duo firsthand and bring updated apps to their users. The enthusiasm has been incredible, and we’re excited to see the pace of updates continue to accelerate as more and more apps optimize for iPhone Duo.”

In total, Apple says that over 2,000 developers have attended more than 50 in-person workshops around the world.

Apple is continuing to spotlight apps for iPhone Duo on the App Store, including editorial curations like “Popular Apps on iPhone Duo” and “Great Games on iPhone Duo.” There’s also a “Made for iPhone Duo” badge that appears on product pages for apps optimized for Apple’s foldable.

Recent apps optimized for iPhone Duo include Microsoft Word, Microsoft Outlook, Zoom, Etsy, Halide Mark III, and more.

I detailed the iPhone Duo app experience in my full review last month. At the time, I emphasized the big difference between using an app updated for iPhone Duo and one that isn’t. I’m thrilled to see how quickly the apps I use every day are being updated for iPhone Duo.

Another trend I’m noticing is that apps that were quick to support iPhone Duo at launch have since received subsequent updates with better optimization for the inner and outer displays.
