#3316. Guarding the Gates of Knowledge

AI can fake a plausible paper at the push of a button. Can detection tools and peer review keep up?

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

A recent scroll through social media got me thinking about trust. About half my feed was filled with AI slop that astute users would call out as being machine-generated, often to the embarrassment of the rube who unknowingly spread it and sometimes to the delight of the poster who shared it deliberately because they found it amusing or useful for sowing confusion.

Remember the good old days of GPT-3 when we could ask the chatbot anything and it would almost instantly and very confidently spit back a plausible but false answer? That’s when the word “hallucination” as applied to AI answers entered the lexicon. Six years and several versions of a few different chatbots later, I still can’t trust the answers I get, even though Claude or Gemini often do useful work for me. That’s the thing about current AI: Trust but verify. And verify you must.

Apply that maxim at scale to maintain the integrity of the scientific record and you get an idea of the challenge facing publishers of peer-reviewed scholarship. In “I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper,” freelance writer and doctor of applied mathematics Benjamin Skuse tells the story of the human gatekeepers trying to beat back the rising tide of AI slop by attempting to get his own AI-generated papers past IEEE’s defenses.

“He basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper.’ And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it.” —Eliza Strickland

As features and AI beat editor Eliza Strickland told me, Skuse was surprised at just how effortless it was to generate a paper that was more or less plausible and more or less science. For one of his experiments, “he basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper,’” she said. “And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it. He just launched it into the maw of the publishing engine.”

Skuse discovered that the combination of IEEE’s human-review processes and research-integrity checker programs are currently keeping pace in what amounts to a cat-and-mouse game against people using free tools. But the more advanced LLMs are no longer making the same dumb mistakes the free versions do. That leaves publishers locked in an arms race between increasingly plausible slop and the systems aimed at detecting it.

Scholarly publishers aren’t the only ones trying to hold the line against slop. So is that global depository of human-generated knowledge, Wikipedia. For this month’s Five Questions, Strickland interviewed Ellia Lebleu, a founding member of WikiProject AI Cleanup, a volunteer effort to detect and delete AI-generated material from the platform. Lebleu’s team is confronting the same problem as commercial publishers, but with fewer people and fewer tools.

“Wikipedia is known as a repository of human-generated information, and they want to hold on to that,” says Strickland. “Who knows how long they’ll be able to do that.”

If we can’t collectively assume that the scientific record is trustworthy or that basic facts about the world are accurate, then our understanding of what is real unspools into uncertainty. Perhaps that delights quantum scientists and the grifters who thrive in an information environment where there is no shared reality. But that uncertainty ultimately undermines trust in the institutions that exist to curate the corpus of human knowledge and to promote the advancement of science and technology for the benefit of humanity.

Or maybe in a world where AI is doing the science and writing the papers, it won’t matter whether or not humans trust the outputs. As Strickland put it, “Doesn’t it just feel crazy that we’ll have AI writing for other AIs at some point? We’ll just get left out of the loop.”

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

#3315. TSMC is weighing a move into AI memory chips at Nvidia’s request

The world's largest chipmaker is drafting plans for 3D DRAM as an AI-driven memory shortage drags on.

The TSMC logo on one of the company’s factories in the Central Taiwan Science Park, Taichung.

TSMC is considering making advanced memory chips and has begun drafting plans for 3D DRAM at Nvidia’s request, The Information reports. It would put TSMC up against Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron as AI demand keeps memory scarce.

TSMC is considering making advanced memory chips, Bloomberg reported on Friday, citing The Information. The move would give the world’s largest chipmaker an even bigger share of the AI hardware supply chain.

TSMC recently began drafting plans to make 3D DRAM, which stacks memory cells vertically to pack in more capacity, at the request of Nvidia, its biggest customer. It could build new factories or buy an existing plant and convert it, Reuters reported, citing The Information.

The work is led by Hsu Kuo-chin, a TSMC vice president who oversees advanced packaging, according to the report. TSMC and Nvidia did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Memory is in short supply as AI data centres soak it up, sending prices soaring. Micron expects the shortage to last into 2028, and Apple raised Mac and iPad prices in June, citing memory costs. Some customers want their own supply: Elon Musk is planning a $55B chip plant to cut his reliance on Micron.

TSMC is already moving closer to memory. In October, Nvidia reportedly asked Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron to build the base layer of its custom HBM memory on TSMC’s 3nm process. Making DRAM itself would put TSMC up against all three, including SK Hynix, which plans to spend $720B on new plants.

#3314. iOS 27.2 adds Apple Photos invisible watermark feature, here’s how it works

iOS 27.2 arrived last week, and among its changes for Apple Photos, the update adds an invisible watermarking feature when you use certain editing tools. Here’s how it works.

In the age of AI, what looks like a genuine photo might actually be a fake—or partly fake. That’s why tools like SynthID have been used to apply invisible watermarks to AI-generated content.

Starting with iOS 27.2, Apple now uses SynthID watermarks when you make AI-generated edits to photos in Apple Photos, or create all-new images with Image Playground.

Starting with iOS 27.2, iPadOS 27.2, macOS 27.2, and visionOS 27.2, some Apple Intelligence tools will add an invisible SynthID watermark to images that you create or edit:

Image Playground generates entirely new images, so it’s more what the average person would consider an “AI image.”

However, as Apple notes, the SynthID invisible watermark is also applied to genuine photos in your Apple Photos library if you use the AI-powered Clean Up, Extend, or Spatial Reframing tools to edit them.

It’s worth emphasizing the word “invisible” here. You won’t see evidence of a watermark anywhere on your photos, nor will others unless they explicitly check the image with a SynthID detector.

If you do want to check for the watermark, Apple recommends going to synthid.com, where you can upload an image and see its result.

How do you feel about Apple Photos adding SynthID watermarks in iOS 27.2? Let us know in the comments.

#3312. MS Direct Lending (MSDL) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Fee cuts and a new dividend framework amid fresh nonaccruals.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Morgan Stanley Direct Lending Fund (MSDL -3.47%) reported third quarter results and announced a reduction in advisory fees to enhance its value proposition for shareholders. Management reported net investment income of $0.48 per share and declared a new supplemental dividend framework to return excess earnings to investors. The company continued to scale the Capstone Joint Venture and utilized its share repurchase program to provide net asset value accretion. While the quarter was impacted by specific credit restructurings and new nonaccruals, management indicated that the broader portfolio maintains stable fundamentals and remains focused on senior secured lending.

Operator: Please stand by. Good day, and welcome to the Morgan Stanley Direct Lending third quarter 2020 Earnings Call. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. A question and answer session will follow the prepared remarks. As a reminder, this conference call is being recorded. At this time, I would like to turn the conference over to Sanna Johnson, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sanna Johnson: Good morning. Welcome to Morgan Stanley Direct Lending Fund's third quarter 26 earnings call. I am joined this morning by Michael Occi, Chief Executive Officer Jeff Day, Co-President David Pessah, chief financial officer and Rebecca Shaoul, head of portfolio management. Morgan Stanley Direct Lending Fund's third quarter 2026 financial results were released yesterday after the market close and can be accessed on the Investor Relations section of our website at www.msdl.com. Have arranged for a replay of today's events that will be accessible from the Morgan Stanley Direct Lending Fund website. During this call, I want to remind you that we may make forward looking statements based on current expectations.

The statements on this call that are not purely historical are forward looking statements. Forward looking statements are not a guarantee of future performance and are subject to uncertainties and other factors that could cause actual results to differ materially from those expressed in the forward looking statements, including without limitation, market conditions, uncertainties surrounding interest rates, changing economic conditions, and other factors we have identified in our filings with the SEC. Although we believe that the assumptions on which these forward looking statements are based are reasonable, any of those assumptions can prove to be inaccurate, and as a result, the forward looking statements based on those assumptions can be incorrect.

You should not place undue reliance on these forward looking statements. The forward looking statements contained on this call are made as of the date hereof, and we assume no obligation to update the forward looking statements or subsequent events. To obtain copies of SEC related filings, please visit our website. With that, I will now turn the call over to Michael Occi.

Michael Occi Jr.: Good morning. And thank you for joining us. I will begin with an overview of the meaningful step we have taken to strengthen MSDL's value proposition for shareholders. Before turning to our third quarter performance. Jeffrey will then cover the market environment and deployment activity, and David will review our financial results in greater detail. We will then open the call for Q&A. We are pleased to announce that the Board has approved a decisive action in our ongoing effort to create value for shareholders. Effective 01/01/2027, we are reducing MSDL's management fee from 100 basis points on assets to 75 basis points on assets, and its incentive fee from 17.5% to 15%.

We believe these reductions will strengthen MSCL's baseline return profile, Combined with our existing incentive fee cap, we believe this makes us a leader on fee structure in the sector. More importantly, this action further strengthens our alignment with shareholders. The fee reduction serves as another proactive step to strengthen MSDL's return profile. And help offset the yield normalization that the industry has experienced over the last several years. We previously established the Capstone joint venture. Increased the size of our share repurchase program, maintained a competitive operating expense profile and optimized our debt stack. The fee reduction is another way to improve shareholder returns while maintaining our disciplined investment mandate.

We have applied this philosophy consistently across our platform, most recently taking a similar action on fees with our non traded BDC offering. The specifics of the improved fee framework were grounded in our objective deliver shareholder value by earning our cost of capital. This move advances that goal, as we believe the per share fee reduction can provide meaningful return accretion. As illustrated in the earnings presentation, on a pro forma basis over the last 12 months, the reduced advisory fees would have increased NII return on NAV by approximately 64 basis points, or approximately $0.03 of quarterly NII per share.

The specific earnings benefit from the lower incentive fee rate will depend on whether the incentive fee cap is in effect, in any given period. This reduction also reinforces our confidence in the durability of the distribution. In addition to declaring the $0.45 regular dividend for the fourth quarter, the Board has declared a quarterly supplemental dividend, which is equivalent to 50% of excess NII per share above the regular dividend. This will be paid during the fourth quarter period resulting in an incremental $0.015 per share for a total distribution yield on NAV of 9.9%. Based on 09/30/2026 NAV per share.

Transitioning now to our third quarter operating results, we generated net investment income of $0.48 per share, compared with $0.45 per share in the prior quarter. Credit indicators were mixed quarter over quarter with the nonaccrual rate increasing modestly and PIK to income declining relative to the second quarter. We did experience mark to market activity, including as a result of 1 realization which led to a decline in NAV in the quarter. Jeffrey will elaborate on this in more detail. Disciplined capital allocation remained a priority in the third quarter. As we navigated the more dynamic market. Continuing our approach from the first half of the year.

We prioritized ramping the JV, and utilizing the buyback and we successfully ended the quarter at what we believe to be near optimal leverage. During the quarter, we continued to scale the Capstone JV including an equity contribution from MSDL of $25 million Because this occurred late in September, this specific step did not meaningfully increase net investment income for the period, However, with this investment, the JV is now approximately 65% utilized and we remain on track to complete the ramp by mid-2027. In our view, there remains a disconnect. Between the direct lending fundamentals and investor sentiment although that gap appears to be gradually narrowing.

To this point, the third quarter saw declining redemption rates at non traded BDCs, including our own. Separating the signal from the noise is admittedly challenging given the 2 distinct realities at play right now in the direct lending market. First, a constructive deployment environment, supported by improved spreads and other lending terms and an upward bias in base rates, and second, pockets of credit softness across the broader market and within MSDL's portfolio. While credit events and dispersion are likely to remain market realities, we believe that the relative value and diversification that this asset class offers for client portfolios remain attractive. Particularly amidst the rate volatility that has challenged public fixed income performance.

We believe this value proposition is enhanced in a wrapper constructed and executed as thoughtfully as MSDL. Our commitment to transparency and alignment with investors is reflected in our actions, including the fee reductions we have outlined today. Leveraging the strength of the Morgan Stanley franchise we believe MSDL remains well positioned to navigate evolving market conditions and deliver long term shareholder value. With that, I will turn the call over to Jeffrey Day.

Jeffrey Day: Thank you, Michael, and good morning. Beginning with the broader direct lending market, we continue to see a favorable environment for disciplined lenders with pricing, documentation, and structural protections remaining meaningfully more attractive than in mid to late 2025. These improvements have proven durable to the third quarter despite continued competition for high quality assets. Our median spread on new deals for the quarter was 38 basis points up from 475 basis points in the prior 2 quarters. Importantly, we are seeing more conservative leverage levels and increased sponsor equity contributions, allowing us to originate loans with more attractive risk adjusted returns and greater structural protections than we were seeing several quarters ago.

From an activity perspective, the market remains somewhat at a crossroads, while overall direct lending volumes remain subdued during the quarter, we have begun to see encouraging signs of renewed M&A interest including within the software sector, where 1 of our existing commitments was taken out as part of a sponsor to sponsor sale process. Private equity sponsors continue to prioritize investment monetization and return of capital to limited partners, which we believe should ultimately support increased transaction activity. At the same time, the Fed's September rate increase and more hawkish outlook introduced an additional headwind for sponsors evaluating new investments and exits.

We believe this dynamic will continue to favor lenders with strong origination relationships, flexible capital and the ability to execute with speed and credibility. Competition remains particularly strong for high quality businesses with durable cash flows, while lenders are demonstrating greater selectivity towards companies facing operational challenges or potential secular disruption. In software specifically, we believe the conversation around AI has become more balanced with increasing recognition that the impact will vary meaningfully by business model. Overall, we remain constructive on the credit fundamentals of our software portfolio while recognizing that the evolving economics of AI reinforce the importance of disciplined underwriting, active portfolio monitoring and investing in market leading businesses with durable competitive positions.

Turning to third quarter activity, MSDL closed 12 investments including 6 new platforms. In addition, the JV balance sheet grew by $132 million which helped further diversify its portfolio and increase earnings. 1 investment to highlight this quarter was Concertis. A global engineering and project advisory platform serving aviation, water, utilities, and technology end markets. initially evaluated the company when RTC Partners acquired it last year but passed given its smaller size. Following a year of strong performance and customer diversification, we are pleased to provide financing for incremental M&A activity. Our underwriting benefited from our team's deep sector experience complemented by differentiated insights from Morgan Stanley's private equity research teams.

The investment was priced as SOFR plus 575 basis points with lender friendly documentation representing an attractive risk adjusted return opportunity for MSDL. Turning to credit, our focus remains on the underlying cash generation and liquidity of our borrowers. While valuation pressure earlier in the year largely reflected broader market concerns around AI disruption and geopolitical uncertainty, recent declines have been driven more by fundamental credit challenges for a limited number of portfolio companies. We believe this softness is not indicative of a deep cycle, but rather we have seen weakness for certain borrowers that reflects idiosyncratic challenges rather than macroeconomic factors such as higher oil prices, weaker consumer demand, or rising base rates.

In particular, we have seen operational and execution challenges at certain highly acquisitive businesses where integration delays cost overruns, and slower than expected synergies have pressured cash flow generation. While these situations warrant close attention, we continue to see stable fundamentals across the broader portfolio without evidence of thematic industry challenges. Against this backdrop and with the potential for higher rates for longer, we remain focused on free cash flow covenant headroom, near term maturities and PIK utilization. We ended the quarter with 5.4% PIK income as a percentage of total income down slightly from the prior quarter and remaining well below the levels observed across our publicly traded BDC peers.

During the quarter, we completed the restructuring of AMCP Pet Holdings, which goes by BrightPet, a manufacturer of premium pet food and treats. Following a deterioration in operating performance driven by company specific operational and execution challenges, ownership of the business was consensually transferred from the sponsor to the lender group. As part of the restructuring, the existing debt was reorganized and the resulting realized loss, while partially offset by the reversal of previously recognized unrealized losses, was the largest contributor to the decline in NAV during the quarter.

While the outcome is disappointing, we believe the challenges at BrightPet are isolated and we are working closely with the management and board to maximize the value of our position over time. In addition to BrightPet, we placed 3 additional investments on nonaccrual during the quarter, representing a $17.2 million at cost. Any Hour and LogRhythm have experienced company specific underperformance for an extended period, while FPG Intermediate HoldCo our afterlife services portfolio company that previously underwent a restructuring, continues to face operational headwinds. Our approach to challenge credits is active and situation specific engaging closely with sponsors and management teams evaluating restructuring alternatives, and maximizing recoveries to preserve shareholder capital.

We remain actively engaged in restructuring discussions for several of our non accrual investments and expect to make further progress towards resolutions over the coming quarters. Importantly, despite these isolated challenges, 93.4% of the portfolio remains in risk rated 1 or 2 assets as of quarter end, underscoring the overall stability of the portfolio. Turning to software. The debate around AI related disruption has become more rational. The discussion is increasingly moving away from broad sector wide assumptions and toward the fundamental of individual companies. Across our own software portfolio, operating performance remains generally healthy supported by continued revenue growth and the detailed company level assessments we have conducted to evaluate potential AI related risks.

Many software businesses are accelerating investments in AI enabled functionality to defend and enhance their competitive positions. Over the near term, we anticipate that this investment along with rising cloud infrastructure and hosting costs, could pressure margin profiles. However, AI driven efficiencies in software development could ultimately help offset some of these incremental expenses. We Through the third quarter, we updated our proprietary AI scorecard which continues to show that only a low single digit percentage of our portfolio is in the category we deem to be at high risk of AI disruption. More broadly, we remain attentive to macroeconomic and geopolitical risks and their potential impact on borrower demand input costs and liquidity.

We continue to stay in close contact with management teams and assess these exposures at individual company level rather than rely on broad sector assumptions. In summary, we continue to see attractive lending opportunities supported by favorable pricing and stronger lender protections even as the operating environment remains challenging for certain borrowers. Our focus remains on disciplined origination, active portfolio management, and preserving shareholder capital while delivering attractive risk adjusted returns. With that, I will turn the call over to David Pessah.

David Pessah: Thank you. Turning to our balance sheet. Our portfolio totaled $3.43 billion at fair value as of quarter end. Our continued focus is at the top of the capital structure with the portfolio being comprised of approximately 96% investments in first lien debt or the JV entity and the remainder in second lien equity and other investments as of September 30. Inclusive of new investment commitments, total investment fundings amounted to approximately $75.1 million during the quarter. Offset by $140.9 million in repayments. We believe the portfolio remains well diversified. With 233 portfolio companies across 37 industries and an average borrower exposure of approximately $14.7 million.

In addition to some of the credit metrics that Jeffrey provided, the weighted average loan to value across our portfolio was approximately 42.4%, and median EBITDA remained relatively unchanged at $91.4 million To provide some additional detail about our JV, the JV has total equity commitments of up to $250 million of which $200 million is committed by MSDL. To date, approximately 65% of the total equity commitments have been called supporting $557 million of investment commitments across portfolio companies in 29 industries. The weighted average yield on debt and income-producing investments is 9.1% at cost.

On a levered basis, the dividend yield on MSDL's investments in the JV equated to approximately 12.9%, Moving to our operating results for the quarter, net investment income was $40.3 million or $0.48 per share, which increased from $38.2 million or $0.45 per share. Total investment income decreased to $86.1 million from $88.8 million The decrease was a function of the impact of positions placed on non accrual and lowered nonrecurring revenue. Total expenses decreased to $45.1 million from $49.8 million in the previous quarter, primarily reflecting lower incentive fees earned which was subject to our incentive fee cap from the restructuring of BrightPet partially offset by higher interest and other financing expenses.

The net change in unrealized depreciation and realized losses for the third quarter was $67.6 million unrealized losses were driven by underperformance in a handful of portfolio companies which includes the aforementioned positions that were placed on nonaccrual. Net realized losses during the period were related to the restructuring of BrightPet. As of September 30, our total assets were $3.59 billion and total net assets were $1.57 billion Our ending NAV per share for the third quarter was $18.76 compared to $19.50 in the prior period. The gross debt to equity ratio closed the quarter at 1.25x, modestly above the 1.21x multiple from the previous quarter.

Additionally, in the third quarter, we proactively refinanced the upcoming February 2027 maturity with a 5-year $350 million unsecured note issuance. While the transaction creates some incremental near term interest expense, it enable us to secure funding ahead of the recent widening in credit spreads and avoid potentially higher borrowing costs had we waited. Overall, we remain confident in the strength and positioning of our debt portfolio through the remainder of 2026 and into 2027. During the period, we repurchased approximately $12.8 million of our shares at prices below NAV, which was $0.04 of accretion to NAV per share. We have approximately $71 million of capacity remaining on the $100 million share repurchase program we refreshed earlier this year.

Regarding distributions, we declared a $0.45 regular distribution for the third quarter. Our Board of Directors declared a $0.45 per share regular distribution for the fourth quarter payable to shareholders of record as of 12/31/2026. and $0.015 per share supplemental distribution payable to shareholders of record as of 11/30/2026. Our spillover income was approximately $0.85 per share. With that, operator, please open the line for questions.

To allow your signal to reach our equipment. Again, that is star 1 if you would like to signal with questions. And the first question will come from Finian O'Shea with Wells Fargo Securities.

Michael Occi Jr.: Hi, Finian. As I alluded to, it really comes down to a reduction of fees, proactive step, to enhance shareholder economics, improve the earnings power, in isolation. #3311. IEEE Computer Society Chapter Offers Webinars With Industry Experts

Attendees in Region 4 learn about AI, cybersecurity, and more

Siva Rama Krishna Varma Bayyavarapu is an IEEE senior member and secretary of the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter.

To help engineers keep up with emerging technologies such as AI, cloud computing, and sustainable infrastructure, and learn how they can be applied in practice, the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter recently launched its Tech Talk Series.

The live webinar series connects IEEE members, undergrad and graduate students, and engineering professionals from IEEE Region 4 with industry practitioners. The monthly sessions have covered AI governance and security, agentic systems, and related topics. The sessions featured speakers from Apple, software company Tavant, and cybersecurity concern Zscaler.

Upcoming sessions and registration details are available on the IEEE Region 4 virtual events calendar.

Rather than presenting on emerging technologies only at a conceptual level, speakers discussed the design decisions behind specific tools and systems, how the systems are structured, and implementation challenges. They also shared lessons learned from using the tools in their daily work.

Sessions also include technical walkthroughs and practical examples.

The live format allows attendees to discuss and compare their approaches when evaluating and implementing new technologies with those used by other organizations.

The organizers chose to make the series virtual so that chapter members and other attendees could participate in technical discussions with engineers from major technology companies and eliminate the need to travel.

For young professionals, the sessions connect what they’ve learned in a classroom with the realities of the workplace.

Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.

Attendees learn how practitioners approach projects such as system architecture, reliability, security, governance, and product delivery. For experienced professionals, the talks offer a forum to examine new ways of designing, securing, and operating software systems, and compare technical approaches. They can ask questions relevant to systems being evaluated or deployed within their organization.

The most recent webinar, Feeding and Fencing AI Agents: Engineering Governed Agentic Systems on Real-Time Data, featured Gajendra Babu Thokala, a senior engineering leader at Apple in Seattle.

The IEEE senior member explained how teams can move beyond adding isolated AI features to applications and instead build governed AI-agent systems that use real-time business data to complete multistep business workflows.

Another recent session, Building AI Native Products: A Playbook for Agentic Systems, explored how products built around AI agents differ from traditional software. It also covered how agentic systems can help users complete multistep tasks and workflows. IEEE Senior Member Sandeep Shivam, a product and technology leader at Tavant in Dallas, led the webinar.

Those two sessions illustrate the series’ purpose: helping participants understand what a technology can do and what is required to use it responsibly.

Future sessions are being planned on areas including enterprise AI, software reliability, and responsible AI usage. In addition to speakers from technology companies, the chapter also plans to invite speakers from startups, universities, and research organizations.

Upcoming sessions are expected to cover cloud platforms, enterprise integrations, and the responsible development of AI systems.

Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.

Undergraduate and graduate students are invited to participate to gain exposure to technical decision-making and challenges encountered in professional engineering environments.

Siva Rama Krishna Varma Bayyavarapu is an IEEE senior member and the secretary of the IEEE Computer Society Central Indiana Chapter. He is also the chair of the IEEE Central Indiana Student Activities Committee.

#3310. Apollo-backed Brightspeed seeks up to $3B from creditors for fibre

The rural broadband provider has about $10B of debt and has warned it may not survive as a going concern.

Fibre optic cables connected to telecommunications equipment in a network rack.

Brightspeed, a US fibre broadband provider owned by Apollo, is in talks with creditors to raise $2B to $3B of new money, Bloomberg reports. It has about $10B of debt, has warned about its survival, and may file for bankruptcy as soon as December.

Brightspeed, an Apollo-backed US fibre broadband provider, is in talks to raise $2B to $3B of new money from its creditors. That is according to Bloomberg, which cited people familiar with the matter on Friday. The amount, and whether the deal will go through a bankruptcy court, are still being worked out.

Brightspeed and Apollo declined to comment. The Wall Street Journal reported last week that the company could file for bankruptcy as soon as December, Light Reading reported.

Brightspeed has about $10B of debt and warned in September that it may not be able to continue as a going concern. Nearly all its debt trades at distressed levels: one $2.5B loan was quoted at about 17 cents on the dollar on Friday.

Brightspeed was formed in 2022, when Apollo bought Lumen’s local phone and broadband business in 20 states for $7.5B. It is spending heavily to bring fibre to mostly rural and suburban areas there. It passed 3 million fibre-ready locations in April, and fibre sales are up 16% from a year earlier.

It has been through this before. In 2024, Brightspeed cut $1.1B of debt and raised $3.7B of new capital in a deal with its lenders. This month, it named Shawn O’Donnell, a former senior managing director at FTI Consulting, as chief executive.

Apollo is better known in tech circles for its lending to AI, including a $36B debt deal it is arranging with Blackstone to buy chips for Anthropic. Lumen, meanwhile, has turned to AI customers, and this week agreed to sell AI networks with Microsoft.

#3309. I tested the Philips Café Aromis 8000 Series — and this superautomatic espresso machine is my biggest $2,000-shaped disappointment of 2026

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Philips Café Aromis 8000 looks beautiful, with a bright, full-color screen and a gorgeous wooden embellishment on the group head. However, it’s outrageously expensive in the U.S. and makes a mid-tasting brew. I would personally skip this one, unless you value appearance over taste.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

I have yet to find a fully automatic espresso machine good enough to earn a permanent place in my kitchen. I’ve tested upwards of twenty now, and they all leave a little to be desired. But nothing’s been quite as disappointing as the Philips Café Aromis 8000 Series… let me explain.

The 8000 Series looks beautiful. It’s easily one of the prettiest superautomatic coffee machines I’ve ever tested. There’s a wood-veneer group head, a cup warmer, and two silver rails on top — just like a commercial espresso machine. My hopes were sky high.

However, I’m not convinced it’s one of the best espresso machines. It’s outrageously expensive in the U.S. ($2k!), makes mid-tasting coffee, and can only make one type of milk texture. I’ll go through all the information in this Philips Café Aromis 8000 Series review.

The Philips Café Aromis 8000 Series is a high-end automatic espresso machine. It’ll set you back $1,999 at Amazon U.S. and £895 at Curry’s U.K.

This is a premium price for a premium machine. Similar options would be the KitchenAid KF8 ($1,999) and the De’Longhi PrimaDonna Aromatic ($2,499).

If $2k is a little too much for you, don’t worry. De’Longhi also makes the $1,499 Rivelia, my favorite superautomatic coffee machine to date. For the money-savvy, there’s also the $795 Terra Kafe Demi, which can’t froth milk, and the Smeg BCC13, which is even cheaper at $749 but doesn’t have a full-color LED screen.

Philips also makes the $394 2200 Series. What’s actually different between the two? Honestly, not as much as you might think. The 2200 Series still has a built-in milk frother, unlike the $795 Terra Kafe Demi, and has a bright screen, unlike the $749 Smeg BCC13. Sure, the 2200 only makes “espresso”, “coffee”, and “hot water”, but that’s the foundation of any coffee drink. While the 8000 Series is much easier thanks to its one-touch recipes, I’m not sure this justifies a whole $1,600 extra. Personally, I would get the $394 2200 Series, or a standalone milk frother, like the $139 Subminimal Nanofoamer Pro Gen 2 for more finesse.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Oh, the Philips Café Aromis 8000 Series is a sight to behold. It’s gorgeous. I’d go so far as to say it’s the most beautiful automatic coffee machine I’ve ever seen. Of course, it’s essentially a big plastic-and-metal box — it’s still an automatic coffee machine, after all — but there’s a sense of finesse missing from other machines (yes, even $2,000 ones).

There’s a cup warmer on top of the machine, complete with two stainless steel rails on either side, and a low-profile grinder. The grinder holds a whole 250g bag of beans at once, even though it’s only rated for 200g.

But my favorite part is the wood finish on the portafilter. Rather than plastic or metal — boring! — the 8000 Series has a gorgeous, glossy wood veneer, making the machine look more like an automatic version of the Lelit MaraX3 than something like the Casabrews Ultra Pro.

You might be sensing a theme here, but it only gets better. Even though the water tank looks pretty small, it’s actually 64 fluid ounces (just under 2 liters). And it’s a slide-out tank, so you don’t need counter space with overhead clearance, unlike the KitchenAid KF3 ($999).

At 15.3 x 9.9 17.8 inches, the 8000 isn’t the slimmest automatic coffee machine I’ve ever tested — that would go to the aforementioned KitchenAid KF3 — but it doesn’t look as bulky as its dimensions might suggest. I had this out in the office for a week (making around ten drinks a day) and it looked right at home.

If you value a good-looking automatic coffee machine, the 8000 is surely for you. I really have nothing bad to say about its appearance.

However, the 8000 Series has “app functionality”. Here’s a screenshot of said “app functionality”.

All you can really do is set user profiles and scroll through recipe ideas — most of which require extra ingredients, like custard or chocolate sauce. While I like that you can customize and save up to 8 drinks for each user profile, I do wish there was more purpose to the app. Sure, you can remote control brewing, but I wish there was something more. Or there’s not much point even having an app.

I also have a bone to pick with the language in said app. As you can see from the screenshots above, the app describes a latte as having “slightly light body, slightly bitter taste”. Coffee shouldn’t actually taste bitter. The central flavor note in a latte should not be bitterness. It should have a little bitterness to balance it out, but the prevailing taste should be fruitiness, chocolate, or nuttiness (depending on your beans). Maybe this is why the coffee tastes mediocre — because the machine is trying to make it bitter.

The standout feature on the 8000 Series is its ease of use. One touch makes 40+ recipes. Some of the recipes I’d never heard of, like Melange and Galão. Of course, there are also a range of cold drinks, but these are extracted hot, so in theory you could pull a normal espresso and top it up with cold milk to achieve the same results.

Here’s a photo of a straightforward espresso.

As you can see, it has a nice layer of crema, but the shot itself is a little pale. This espresso tasted rich and smooth, but with a little too much bitterness at the back of the palate for my personal taste.

You can easily customize the espresso settings for every drink (and then save your customized drinks to profiles). You can adjust the strength from 1-7, temperature, and use ground coffee if you please.

The grinder is also manually adjustable, but the machine calibrated itself based on my beans. Pressing the bean button brings up a built-in AI, which asks questions about roast and species of bean. After I provided this information, it adjusted the grind size to suit.

I found most drinks were way too bitter by default. I like the taste of coffee — I drink straight espresso to taste-test every single coffee machine. However, the 8000 Series brought out an unpleasant bitter note in my usual Ethiopian, medium-roasted testing beans, so I had to increase milk volume for every drink recipe.

The oat flat white (pictured in the “Milk” section below) was almost black. This is incredibly weird. I would recommend adjusting the default recipe for each drink to ensure it’s not overly strong.

I appreciate the 8000 Series comes with both a hot and cold milk frother — more versatile than the De’Longhi Rivelia, which makes you spend extra for the cold milk system. However, you can’t customize the milk texture at all. You can adjust milk volume, but not texture. Iced latte, hot cappuccino, flat white, macchiato… all the same milk texture.

I’m sure the drinks are intended to be different milk textures, but they’re not. Everything is a little too aerated. There’s also no non-dairy/dairy milk setting, so oat milk is treated the same as cow milk, which is disappointing to see on such a pricey machine.

Here are three photos: one is an oat flat white, one is a cow milk latte, and one is an oat layered latte.

As you can see, the milk texture is relatively similar, and describable in one word: bubbly. For a $2,000 machine, it’s just not good enough. De’Longhi’s high-end milk systems allow for a three-prong customizer: you can choose low, medium, or high foam.

So, while I value the inclusion of a cold milk frother, the said milk frother isn’t as effective as De’Longhi’s “LatteCrema” systems.

At 10 inches wide, 18 inches deep, and 15 inches tall, this is no small machine. However, it doesn’t require any overhead clearance thanks to the flush grinder hopper and side-accessible water tank, so you could theoretically get it even if your counters only have 16 inches of space.

The 8000 Series comes with a water filter, which I’d recommend installing regardless of water hardness. If you live in a particularly hard water area, you will need to descale more often than the machine recommends. Don’t worry if you don’t know your water hardness — the machine comes with a test strip.

Philips makes a descaler: $16 for two packs at Amazon. This should last you around six months depending on your water hardness.

Cleaning is also easy: the milk frothers and drip tray are dishwasher safe (but they take up a lot of space in said dishwasher), and the machine will alert you when you need to rinse internal brewing elements. Be warned that coffee grounds go moldy quickly, so empty this at least every day.

Finally, warranty. Philips offers a 2-year standard warranty, which is the same as KitchenAid, De’Longhi, Ninja, and Breville. I’d like to see coffee companies start to move towards a 5-year warranty, especially when these machines cost so much.

I really don’t think the Philips Café Aromis 8000 Series is worth $2,000. It tastes like coffee you can get on the $394 2200 Series. If you really, really want to spend two grand, I’d recommend the KitchenAid KF8 instead. If you want to save money but get an automatic machine, I’d go for the $1,400 De’Longhi Rivelia or $895 Smeg BCC13.

While the Café Aromis 8000 Series looks gorgeous and is incredibly easy to use, I cannot find anything to justify that price. Sure, it can make 40+ recipes, but are you really going to make a Melange or Galão on a fully automatic coffee machine? Not really. Just make it manually — it’ll taste better. As the machine can’t actually make different milk textures, it’s not a true Melange or Galão anyway.

I would personally skip this one. It’s much too expensive in the U.S. and doesn’t make nice-tasting coffee — but if you value appearance and ease of use over anything else, you might not be disappointed.

Erin Bashford is a senior writer at Tom's Guide, focusing on reviews. She has a Masters in Broadcast and Digital Journalism from the University of East Anglia. As an ex-barista, she knows her way around a coffee machine, and as a music lover, she's constantly chipping away at her dream of having a multi-room home sound system. #3308. Next year’s iPhone Pro redesign will drop an important button, per leak

Next year Apple is rumored to have a big redesign coming to the iPhone Pro models, and per a new leak, it may come with the loss of the Action button.

2027 brings the iPhone’s 20th anniversary, and all signs indicate Apple has something special planned. Similar to the debut of iPhone X for the 10th anniversary in 2017, Apple may introduce a bold new iPhone design next year.

New iPhone Pro models are rumored to get quad-curved displays that wrap around the edges for a visually bezel-free appearance. Screen size is expected to increase too.

Now today, a new post from leaker Instant Digital on Weibo says this new design will also come with a loss.

Per the post, the Action button will be removed from next year’s iPhone Pro models. The devices will retain a Camera Control button though, similar to iPhone Duo.

I know quite a few people a decade ago who got the phones with curved screens. All it does is cause you to accidently hit stuff with your palm. Really hope this isn't true.

The leaker says the Action button’s functionality won’t be lost altogether, though. Instead, he says Camera Control will continue to launch the Camera app with a standard press, but a long-press will offer Action button-like functionality.

When iPhone Duo dropped the Action button, some users expressed disappointment that the button’s versatility was lost. Our own Chance Miller, for example, said he would gladly give up Camera Control to keep the Action button.

It sounds like Apple plans to integrate the two, a pattern that will likely apply to the next-generation iPhone Duo and other future models too.

What do you think of Apple’s reported plan for the Action button? Let us know in the comments.

#3307. Musk says government work will be under 10% of SpaceX revenue

AI computing, led by Anthropic, has overtaken NASA and the Pentagon as SpaceX's main source of money.

Elon Musk at VivaTech in Paris, 16 June 2023

Elon Musk said government contracts will make up less than 10% of SpaceX’s revenue this quarter, down from 16.6%. SpaceX now earns most from renting AI computing, with Anthropic its biggest customer, though Anthropic can exit from early 2027.

Government contracts will make up less than 10% of SpaceX’s revenue this quarter, Elon Musk said on X, Bloomberg reported on Friday. That is down from 16.6% in the third quarter and roughly a fifth in 2025.

Musk said the share would fall below 5% about a year from now, Reuters reported. NASA and the Pentagon were long SpaceX’s most important customers, paying it to launch astronauts and national security satellites.

The money now comes from AI. In the third quarter, SpaceX’s AI unit brought in $7.56B, more than Starlink, mostly by renting out computing power from its data centres in Memphis. Anthropic alone accounted for 34.5% of revenue, making it SpaceX’s biggest customer.

That brings its own risk. Anthropic can exit its contracts with 90 days’ notice from early 2027, and Wall Street has recently soured on companies that rent out AI computing, Bloomberg said. Musk himself warned last month that few will survive without other sources of revenue.

Musk’s comments came days after Democrats won control of both houses of Congress. He spent more than $445M backing Republicans, most of whom lost, and Bloomberg said that could strain his companies’ ties with the new Congress. SpaceX still holds a NASA contract to land astronauts on the Moon with Starship as early as 2028.

#3306. Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras

With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery

Advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated. The techniques reveal fine details in the sun’s corona, which is white in this image. The tiny pink shapes seen along portions of the edge of the blacked-out solar disk are prominences, which are extensions of relatively cool plasma that can jut out hundreds of thousands of kilometers into space.

The sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain. But from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza, it appears that a few puffy white clouds have started to block the sun. That’s vexing.

A group of researchers, some wearing cardboard eclipse glasses, is clustered around sets of portable telescopes and cameras connected to laptops. All this gear is scattered on tabletops perched on the mountainside. On the computer screens, the sun’s disk looks like a deep orange crescent that is slowly waning. That’s because the moon began to crawl across it about half an hour ago. In 25 minutes, it will obscure the sun completely, producing an eerie and wondrous phenomenon—a total solar eclipse.

In the late-summer, late-afternoon heat, the researchers watch anxiously as those fluffy clouds linger around the sun. From an abandoned hut on the slope a few meters above, where the researchers have set up camp, one of the grad students emerges and nods toward the cloud formation. “Do you think it will dissolve?” he blurts out.

“It will.” Miloslav Druckmüller glances calmly at his group of doctoral candidates, now making final checks of the equipment in preparation for totality. Here in Spain, on this 12th day of August, Druckmüller is getting ready for his 19th solar eclipse. He knows from long experience that weather can turn quickly when the moon’s shadow suddenly pushes the temperature down. Plus, there’s no sense in riling up the grad students any more than they already are.

Miloslav Druckmüller led the design and construction of a unique optical instrument that incorporates eight astrocameras. Each is equipped with a spectral filter for sensing and recording specific emission spectra from the solar corona. Each of those spectra, in turn, is associated with a particular ionic species of iron atoms. Because the temperature needed to ionize iron varies depending on the ionic species, analyzing the locations and relative abundance of these ionic species offers valuable insights into the distribution of heat in the corona.Václav Široký

During totality, the moon blocks the overwhelming glare of the solar disk, revealing delicate structures in the sun’s outer atmosphere, the corona. Using custom-built telescope systems and image-processing techniques that Druckmüller has spent decades developing, the researchers aim to gain insights into the processes in this enigmatic region that is otherwise hard to study. In addition to imaging the visible coronal light, the team will try to track the dispersal of superhot ions of iron into interplanetary space, which could give rare insights into the pattern of heat emanating from the corona.

And they’ll have 107 seconds to do all that.

Druckmüller is a professor of mathematics and image processing at the Brno University of Technology in the Czech Republic and a leading figure in the Solar Wind Sherpas, an international team that studies the sun’s corona during total eclipses. In the solar eclipse world, he is nothing short of a legend, albeit a reluctant one.

An image from Miloslav Druckmüller’s first solar-eclipse expedition, to Hungary, vividly shows Baily’s Beads. These elongated white lights along a piece of the left edge of the blacked-out solar disk are caused by beams of sunlight shining through gaps in the irregular lunar surface during the eclipse. The pink shapes are solar prominences, which are jets of plasma extending out into space and held in place by the sun’s intense magnetic field.

He photographed his first solar eclipse in 1999, in what he thought would be a one-off lark. During that eclipse, the moon’s deep shadow missed Druckmüller’s native Czechia by just a few tens of kilometers, so he chased it to Hungary with a 30-year-old Soviet MTO 1,000-millimeter lens. All he remembers from that day is the rush of adrenaline he felt while trying to find the sun in the sky with the lens’s minuscule field of view and keep it in focus for the two minutes of the eclipse.

He insists that he has never enjoyed any of the eclipses he has photographed. “In fact, I have never properly seen any of those eclipses. You are just watching the screens, making sure that it’s all doing what it’s supposed to do. There are so many things that can go wrong and you can’t redo it.”

A composite sequence of photographs shows the 12 August 2026 solar eclipse as seen from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain.

Despite Druckmüller’s outward tranquility on this Spanish hillside, the stakes are high. Just 45 minutes ago, his group heard from their colleagues in Iceland, where viewing conditions had promised to be better than in Spain. But a vast low-pressure system had clouded the entire sky, leaving all three Iceland teams without a view.

On the Pico Trigaza mountain in Spain, two postgraduate researchers used a laser to get a rough, initial alignment for the tracking mount of an optical instrument. The alignment was necessary to precisely compensate for the Earth’s motion.

The corona has been a mystery for centuries. Though dimmer—by a factor of a million—than the sun’s visible surface, the corona is nevertheless extremely hot: about a million degrees Celsius compared to 5,500 degrees on the surface. Because the sun’s nuclear fusion engine churns at the star’s heart, it might seem that temperatures should fall farther from the core.

To observe the faint corona in visible light, researchers must block the sun’s ferocious glare. Specialized telescopes called coronagraphs do this with an opaque disk called an occulter. But because light bends around the occulter’s edges in an effect called diffraction, it must block an area much larger than that of the solar disk to prevent light from spilling over and ruining the images. But doing so means obstructing the inner part of the corona, which harbors the most important processes that underpin the puzzling phenomena of the sun’s upper atmosphere.

That’s why total eclipses matter so much to solar physicists. By sheer chance, the moon is exactly the right size and at just the right distance to completely cover the sun during a total solar eclipse. Because the moon is so far away from Earth, the view is not marred by diffraction, and the corona reveals itself nearly all the way down to the sun’s surface.

As astrocameras recorded spectral data about the sun’s corona, a laptop computer [on table, at left] displayed the phase of the eclipse.

Space probes can image the solar surface in other wavelengths, but those views have limitations, too. Spacecraft such as NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory do see the innermost parts of the corona in extreme ultraviolet light, explains Shadia Habbal, a solar physicist at the University of Hawaii and leader of the Solar Wind Sherpas project. “But it cuts off very quickly, so you don’t see its extension into space as well as we can see it in the visible emission lines” during an eclipse. “That’s the biggest advantage,” she says, of solar eclipse photography.

The European Proba-3 mission, launched in 2024, simulates total solar eclipses by flying two spacecraft in a formation 150 meters apart with one acting as an occulter and the other as the telescope. The instruments aboard that satellite, however, have limitations compared to the equipment used by the Solar Wind Sherpas team.

When Druckmüller developed the film from his 1999 eclipse expedition, the photographs didn’t do justice to the event’s eerie beauty. He spent countless evenings applying his expertise in numerical image processing in an attempt to re-create in his photographs the sights he witnessed in that Hungarian corn field.

It took two years, but eventually he succeeded. Where before there were dull views of the blackened lunar disk surrounded by the blunt wisps of the corona, Druckmüller revealed the subtlest details of the magnetic field lines stretching from the sun far into space. As his photographs circulated among solar physicists, invitations to eclipse expeditions began to arrive.

Solar researchers Miloslav Druckmüller and Shadia Habbal have been collaborating for two decades and 15 eclipses.

Habbal learned about the images from a Ph.D. student who had seen them at a conference presentation that didn’t credit Druckmüller. When Habbal’s team later published the images in a paper, they misattributed them to another researcher. Druckmüller found out through an astrophysicist friend. “I wrote her a rather disappointed email and she responded within 10 minutes,” Druckmüller recalls. “She really didn’t have a clue.”

The error was corrected, and within weeks, Habbal and Druckmüller began a collaboration that grew into a friendship. “Milos’s processing brings out details that nobody has seen before, and they tell you a lot about very tiny features in the corona that you don’t see otherwise,” says Habbal.

Capturing the corona’s delicate structures means finding a way to show its brightest and faintest features in the same image. “During the solar eclipse, the contrast between the darkest and brightest parts of the corona is enormous, possibly one to a million,” Druckmüller explains. “But a computer monitor only allows you to display a contrast ratio of one to about 800.” (Some modern monitors, particularly OLED ones, can deliver higher contrast ratios.)

The human eye can adjust to this enormous range of brightness, allowing an observer to see both the bright corona and the faint stars and planets that briefly emerge in the darkened sky. To bring those details together in a photograph, Druckmüller uses custom image-processing algorithms to combine exposures that capture different parts of that range.

Researchers Martin Šebek and Peter Urgoš make fine adjustments to the focus and alignment of the astrocameras on a key optical instrument before the 12 August solar eclipse.

To create a single image, Druckmüller’s teams need to take 200 individual frames during the eclipse at exposure times ranging from 0.001 second to two seconds. The data must then be calibrated against a vast number of reference images to filter out noise and imperfections. Flat fields, which depict a uniform light background, help correct for defects caused by telescope optics, dust spots, and variations in pixel sensitivity. Dark frames, taken with light blocked from the sensor, help correct for artifacts created by the camera’s image sensor itself. “It takes the computer more than two days to process one image,” Druckmüller says. Including the calibration data, a single finished image requires about 3,000 input frames.

Since 2008, teams directed by Habbal and Druckmüller have traveled to every total solar eclipse, spreading out across multiple locations to hedge against bad weather. About half of the teams return with usable data. For the others, it’s just a short and stressful voyage. For the 12 August eclipse, three groups deployed to Iceland and two to Spain.

The teams seek sites close to the center of the band of totality, where the moon blocks the sun for longest. In Spain, the 12 August band of totality cut across the north of the country; the center line of the shadow passed within 11 kilometers of Pico Trigaza, promising Druckmüller and his colleagues a precious 107 seconds of totality.

But duration is only part of the calculation. Totality on Pico Trigaza will commence 51 minutes before sunset, with the sun just 8 degrees above the horizon. That low, the rays must pass through a much thicker layer of the atmosphere than when the sun is higher in the sky, increasing the light distortion that complicates photography. At the researchers’ camp on Pico Trigaza, 1,600 meters above sea level, the thinner air should help a bit.

An abandoned hut on the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain was spruced up so that it could serve as a home base for the research team recording the 12 August solar eclipse.

“Iceland would have been a much better place for us than Spain because the sun was higher up, some 25 degrees above the horizon,” Druckmüller says wistfully. But Iceland’s notoriously unpredictable weather made Spain an essential backup.

If you pack a van with thousands of dollars’ worth of cameras and optical gear and then set out on a 2,351-kilometer journey, you shouldn’t be surprised if you finish the trip with a few striking photographs [top]. The sleeping arrangements for the grad students at the Pico Trigaza hut [bottom] were spartan, but the views were first-rate.Top: Martin Šebek; Bottom: Václav Široký

On the mountain, locals have spruced up a rustic, long-unused hut for the researchers, running power cables from a nearby telecommunication outpost and bringing in a water tank. Five Ph.D. students drove more than 2,000 kilometers from Brno and have spent nearly a week preparing the equipment. Druckmüller and his wife joined them two days before the eclipse. They cook on a small propane grill and sleep in sleeping bags on yoga mats. “We have plenty of space here to set up our telescopes, beautiful views, and a roof over our heads,” Druckmüller says with a grin. “It’s perfect.”

But even the best equipment and a carefully chosen site count for nothing if the clouds roll in. “So much work goes into the preparations and then, if you end up with nothing, you just feel terrible sadness,” says Jana Hoderová, an assistant professor of mathematics at Brno University of Technology and one of Druckmüller’s key collaborators.

As the moon continues to slide in front of the solar disk, the pesky cumulus cloud that kept everybody on edge begins to dissolve. It’s 10 minutes to totality. The relief is palpable.

The countdown on the computers that control the cameras has begun. The screens are now showing only a tiny orange sliver, and the evening is becoming perceptibly less bright.

Twenty astrophotography cameras, most of them drawing power from a car battery that was also buffering the cameras from any grid instabilities, are pointed at the sun. Alongside equipment capturing the corona’s visible light, the team has built an assembly of eight cameras to detect light emitted by various iron ions that arise in the corona.

Among the optical gear assembled at Pico Trigaza to capture the 12 August solar eclipse was a unique instrument designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona [at left]. Václav Široký

Those instruments looking for iron ions have been put together with resourcefulness and thrift. A colleague of Druckmüller’s laser-cut the aluminum plates holding the carefully aligned lenses in exchange “for two bottles of whisky.” The brackets and attachments were 3D-printed at Brno University of Technology. The lenses, produced for the defunct camera maker Contax, were bought at steep discounts on eBay. By far the most expensive elements are interference filters that isolate the wavelengths emitted by the iron ions.

Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still.

“That’s something nobody else in the world can do,” Druckmüller says with visible satisfaction. The unique technology, codeveloped with Habbal’s Hawaii team, has already enabled researchers to map the distribution of temperatures across the entire corona and to discover previously unseen structures, dubbed “smoke rings,” in the coronal plasma. The photographs also revealed the boundary region where the solar plasma becomes so thin that its ions stop colliding.

The optical assembly designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona is outfitted with astrocameras, each of which captures spectra from a different ionic species. To do that, each astrocamera is equipped with a spectral filter whose bandwidth is so narrow—one nanometer—that the filter appears as a mirror.Martin Fornůsek

“Iron is the most abundant of the heavy elements that we see in the solar corona,” says Habbal. “And because the corona is so hot, the iron atoms lose electrons and get ionized. The larger the loss, the higher the temperature.”

For example, a temperature of around 1.6 million °C is necessary to produce an iron ion that has lost 12 electrons. But only 1.4 million °C is needed to strip an iron atom of 11 electrons. Once it’s in a particular electrical state, the ion retains its specific ionization, even as it travels outward with the solar wind. Each of those ions, whether +11 or +12, emits a different wavelength of light, allowing the researchers to map not just temperatures within the corona, but also how those iron ions spread into interplanetary space and distribute heat. Habbal and her colleagues had long been trying to image those iron ions during solar eclipses. But it wasn’t until Druckmüller entered the picture that they were able to develop the gear and the mathematical techniques to do it.

With just a minute to go to totality, the researchers begin removing protective filters from the lenses. It’s 50 minutes to sunset, and the waning sun has just begun to light up the clouds above the horizon with the first tinge of orange. Then, suddenly, the evening begins a rapid and premature descent into darkness. Along the edge of the fantastically thin solar crescent, the brilliant orange points known as Baily’s Beads flash and disappear—the last fragments of photospheric light visible through deep lunar valleys. As totality begins, observers remove their glasses. The hot air cools. The graduate students remain quietly and intently focused on their gear.

Druckmüller looks up from his camera toward the darkened plains. Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still. The sky is ablaze with fiery colors all along the horizon where the deep lunar shadow drops off. Venus burns brilliantly in the southwest, a sharp white pinpoint in the darkened sky. The sound of camera shutters suddenly fills the air. Then, as quickly as it fell, the darkness begins to recede, bid farewell with another handful of golden Baily’s Beads.

The crowd erupts in cheers. The Ph.D. students throw themselves at each other and hug like they mean it.

“The students did most of the work this time, so I actually allowed myself to really look at it,” Druckmüller says. “It was beautiful. Pico Trigaza may not have been the best for science photography, but from the aesthetic point of view, it was extraordinary.”

The 2026 solar-eclipse team at Pico Trigaza in Spain included [from left] Magdalena Šrotířová, Peter Urgoš, Martin Fornůsek, Miloslav Druckmüller, Václav Široký, and Martin Šebek.Václav Široký

But for Druckmüller, this is just the beginning. While other eclipse chasers will race to release their images, he will take his time. He expects to publish the first visible-light images of the corona in about two weeks. Processing the iron-ion images, and uncovering whatever insights they may hold, will take months—maybe even a whole year.

“Probably until the next eclipse in 2027” in North Africa, Druckmüller says.

Who knows? Maybe he’ll even enjoy that one, too.

Tereza Pultarova is a London-based journalist specializing in aerospace and defense technologies. She is a native of the Czech Republic.

Those are some pretty impressive photos! It also seems like the iron ion filtering is pretty unique. I love seeing cases where people build something they want to see in the world with minimal outside support. Seems like it would be a solid return on more public money to seek out and support scrappy projects like this one.

#3305. Fidelity (FNF) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Investments and a sharp October order drop tested title margins.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Fidelity National Financial, Inc. (FNF +2.21%) reported quarterly results supported by record commercial title performance and growth in its F&G annuities segment. Management reported that the title segment generated an industry-leading 17.1% margin despite a low-transaction environment in residential real estate driven by elevated mortgage rates. The company is managing through the current cycle by focusing on operational discipline and long-term investments in technology and recruitment. Management stated that the F&G segment has surpassed $75 billion in assets under management before reinsurance, contributing 22% of the company's adjusted net earnings for the first nine months of the year. The company continues to prioritize capital returns, having returned $561 million to shareholders year to date through dividends and share repurchases.

Existing home sales continue to reflect a low transactional environment due to mortgage rates and housing market dynamics.

Mortgage rates remain high, but have fallen from the recent peak following the Federal Reserve rate hike in September. This is the opposite of the trend we saw in 2025,, and has amplified the normal seasonal decline. Over the course of the year, purchase orders opened have held up well through August, with each month comparing favorably to the prior year, before falling behind by 2% for the month of September. Importantly, we continue to steadily outperform relative to our peers. For the quarter, our daily purchase orders opened were up 3% over the third quarter of 2025, down 9% from the second quarter of 2026 and down 6% for the month of October versus the prior year.

Our residential refinance volumes continue to be responsive to 30 year mortgage rates, although accounting for only 6% of our direct revenue in the third quarter. Notably, we have demonstrated our ability to generate strong adjusted pretax title margins without a substantial refinance market over the past 5 years. Refinance orders opened were 1.4 thousand per day in the third quarter, as compared to 1.6 thousand in both the prior year and sequential quarters. Given mortgage rates in October, we saw refinance orders opened decreased to 1.2 thousand per day reflecting how refinance volumes can quickly change with moves in rates.

Our refinance orders opened per day were down 11% from the third quarter of 2025, down 7% from the second quarter of 2026, and down 35% for the month of October versus the prior year. Our commercial business is on pace for a record year. Direct commercial revenue was $1.2 billion in the first 9 months, up 22% over $1 billion in the first 9 months of 2025. National and local market daily orders opened trended down 1% and up 6%, respectively, in the third quarter as compared to the prior year quarter.

Total commercial orders opened were 876 per day, up 2% over the third quarter of 2025 down 5% from the second quarter of 2026 and down 6% for the month of October versus the prior year. We closed 24 transactions generating over $1 million each in premiums in the third quarter across multiple asset classes. In both our direct and agency businesses. This is reflected in our higher trending commercial fee per file. We view the current momentum in commercial as sustainable over the near term. Our commercial strength continues to be broad based, across both geographies and asset classes.

The composition of our commercial pipeline remains healthy and includes a mix of industrial, data centers, multifamily, affordable housing, retail and energy transactions. At this time, we expect office to gradually recover with top tier properties leading the rebound. 1 question that I often receive is around data centers. We have seen data center transactions in our pipeline over the past 4 years. And in some cases have already seen refinances of transactions that close between 2022 and 2024 which is an underappreciated demand driver. Similar to energy, data centers tend to be higher premium transactions although comprising a small portion of the overall order count.

This shows up in our national fee per file which benefits from the larger energy and data center deals. To bring it all together, total orders opened averaged 5.8 thousand per day in the third quarter, with July at 5.9 thousand August at 5.8 thousand and September at 5.6 thousand. For the month of October, total orders opened were 4.7 thousand per day down 17% from the prior year. Looking to the fourth quarter, we remain optimistic about our commercial momentum although we recognize the impact on residential purchase and refinance volumes of elevated mortgage rates and the typical fourth quarter seasonality.

All else equal, we would expect our adjusted pretax title margin to move toward the lower end of our 15%-20% normal range in the fourth quarter. Over time, as mortgage rates eventually improve, we believe residential purchase and refinance activity will accelerate and trend toward historical levels. This recovery represents additional earnings power given the operational leverage that we have built into our model. This operational leverage is also supported by the investments we continue to make in technology and AI. FNF provides essential services that extend well beyond the title insurance policy we also manage the settlement process from start to finish. We are the rails on which real estate transactions run.

For years, we have invested with the vision of building a differentiated technology platform with 1 overarching objective, to make every real estate transaction faster safer, and simpler. That objective is showing up in what we are delivering today. Since we rolled out our partnership with Clear last year, we have run nearly 100 thousand enhanced identity verifications across our operations to counter impersonation and wire fraud in property sales. Since we launched property monitoring earlier this year, we have provided visibility and alerts as a complementary service to over 250 thousand homeowners after closing. We continue to receive positive feedback from our customers on this value add service.

We are accelerating our property monitoring rollout and we expect it to become the largest footprint in the industry. We are also driving deeper digital engagement with nearly 88% adoption of inHere across eligible residential sale transactions. That is the foundation. AI is the next layer. We are already deploying AI driven agents into production workflows, to improve speed and execution across the Title I settlement process This is not a pilot. it is operational. AI is still early, but the direction is clear. A better experience for our customers and higher productivity for us.

Combined with our broader technology investments, these capabilities strengthen our competitive position and our ability to consistently deliver industry leading adjusted pretax title margins over time. Turning now to our F and G segment. F and G's assets under management before reinsurance have surpassed the $75 billion milestone at September 30. Gross AUM of $76.2 billion was up 7% over the prior year quarter. F and G continues to expand its retail and institutional franchises and delivered its best core retail sales quarter in history. Opportunistic sales intentionally lower due to returns below threshold, as F and G continues to allocate capital to the highest return opportunities.

On a stand alone basis, FNG reported GAAP equity excluding AOCI of $6.7 billion at quarter end. And has grown its book value per share excluding AOCI to $51.37, up 87% since the 2020 acquisition. At recent levels, the FG stock has an especially attractive dividend yield of around 5%. Which is above average for the publicly traded life and annuity sector.

#3303. Microsoft is winding down its deal to rent AI computing from Oracle

The rented servers ran older Nvidia chips, and Microsoft is rethinking billions in outside cloud deals.

The Microsoft logo on the side of one of its office buildings.

Microsoft is winding down a 2023 deal to rent AI computing from Oracle after declining to renew it, Bloomberg reports. The servers ran older Nvidia chips. Microsoft is reassessing more than $80B in contracts with outside cloud providers.

Microsoft is winding down a deal to rent AI computing power from Oracle, Bloomberg reported on Friday, citing people familiar with the matter. Microsoft has been switching off the rented capacity in recent months after deciding not to renew the contract.

The servers ran older Nvidia chips and no longer matched what Microsoft needed, the people said. Ageing hardware is a growing worry: Gartner has warned that much AI infrastructure spending could face large write-downs as newer chips arrive.

The deal, announced in 2023, gave Microsoft Oracle servers to run its AI-powered Bing search, and Bloomberg could not determine its full size. Separate talks for Microsoft to lease more Oracle capacity collapsed in June, Business Insider reported.

Microsoft declined to comment. Oracle said demand for its AI infrastructure remains strong, including for older chips, and its shares fell about 3%.

Microsoft has committed more than $80B to rent capacity from other cloud firms such as CoreWeave, Nscale and Nebius. Its leaders have grown frustrated with their costs and delays, Bloomberg said. This week, it reportedly turned down an option to expand a Nscale deal in Texas, weeks after pulling out of a Nscale site in the UK.

The news adds to Oracle’s troubles. Heavy spending on AI data centres has pushed its free cash flow negative and its credit rating to one notch above junk. Its shares have more than halved since a June peak.
